Q1010972.bio: Glaucias was a Greek physician of the Empiric school who wrote commentaries on the works of Hippocrates.

Q101240374.bio: ancient Greek historian, probably author of a local history of Achaia

Q10133.bio: Gaius Suetonius Tranquillus, commonly referred to as Suetonius, was a Roman historian who wrote during the early Imperial era of the Roman Empire.

Q1024531.bio: Xenocles was an ancient Greek tragedian. He won a victory at the Dionysia in 415 BCE with the plays Oedipus, Lycaon, and Bacchae with the satyr play Athamas.

Q1025360.bio: Caecilia Trebulla was a poet of the Roman Empire, about whom little is known. She may have been an aristocrat based on assumptions made about the nature of her writing and knowledge of literary Greek.

Q10261.bio: Pythagoras of Samos was an ancient Ionian Greek philosopher, polymath, and the eponymous founder of Pythagoreanism. His political and religious teachings were well known in Magna Graecia and influenced the philosophies of Plato, Aristotle, and, through them, Western philosophy.

Q102731250.bio: ancient Greek comic poet lived between 3rd and 2nd century B.C

Q10291533.bio: Gregory of Corinth, born George Pardos, was a Byzantine Greek writer, grammarian and clergyman who served as the metropolitan of Corinth from 1092.

Q1033012.bio: Candidus Isaurus (fl. 491) was an Eastern Roman historian.

Q1036270.bio: Hieronymus of Rhodes was a Peripatetic philosopher, and an opponent of Arcesilaus and Lyco of Troas. Only a few fragments of his works survive, preserved in the quotations of later writers.

Q10371645.bio: Simeon II or Symeon II was a Greek Orthodox patriarch of Jerusalem in the 11th century. Simeon was appointed patriarch in the 1080s.

Q104580055.bio: ancient Greek historian, author of a work on the history of Italy

Q104708245.bio: Asclepiades of Cyprus was a historian of ancient Greece, who wrote a work on the history of his native island and Phoenicia, of which a fragment is preserved by the philosopher Porphyry. Some scholars have suggested that he was Phoenician instead of Cyprian.

Q104712670.bio: ancient Greek historian, author of a work entitled Ἰταλικά

Q104915222.bio: ancient Greek historian, author of a work on Macedonian kings

Q1049225.bio: Rufus of Ephesus was a Greek physician and author who wrote treatises on dietetics, pathology, anatomy, gynaecology, and patient care.

Q105103741.bio: historian cited by Diodorus on Assyrian history

Q1051470.bio: Vettius Valens (February 8, 120 - c. 175) was a 2nd-century Hellenistic astrologer, a somewhat younger contemporary of Claudius Ptolemy.

Q105225061.bio: ancient Greek historian, chronicler of Knidos

Q105290.bio: Praxiteles of Athens, the son of Cephisodotus the Elder, was the most renowned of the Attic sculptors of the 4th century BCE. He was the first to sculpt the nude female form in a life-size statue.

Q1056125.bio: Iccus of Taranto (5th century BCE) was a Magna Grecia Olympic athlete, a victor during the 84th Games (444 BCE) or 70th Games (470 BCE) according to older sources. He is considered the father of athletic dietology.

Q105687254.bio: Numenius of Heraclea is ancient Greek physician and poet, dated to the end of the 4th century BCE. According to Athenaeus, he was a pupil of the physician Dieuches. The author is registered in the TLG Canon as tlg0703.

Q1057344.bio: Hedylus was a Greek epigrammatic poet of the Hellenistic period.

Q1057347.bio: Hegesander was an ancient Greek historian, and a citizen of Delphi. Besides an historical work, called Commentaries, which consisted of at least six books, and seems to have been of a somewhat discursive character, he wrote a work on statues (hypomnema andrianton kai agalmaton).

Q1057422.bio: Heraclitus was a grammarian and rhetorician, who wrote a Greek commentary on Homer which is still extant.

Q105744809.bio: one or several ancient Greek historians

Q105780567.bio: ancient Greek historian on Phoenician affairs, lives of philosophers

Q106427839.bio: Marinos Tzanes, also known as Marinos Tzanes Bounialis, was a Greek painter and poet. His most notable work, The Cretan War, was printed in 1681 and is over six hundred pages long.

Q1073837.bio: Critolaus (; Greek: Κριτόλαος Kritolaos; c. 200 - c.

Q1075807.bio: Choerilus of Samos was an epic poet of Samos, who flourished at the end of the 5th century BCE.

Q1075809.bio: Choerilus was an Athenian tragic poet, who exhibited plays as early as 524 BCE. Choerilus started writing tragedies when he was 22 years old. He staged 160 plays and won the prize 13 times.

Q108865085.bio: author of a lost history of Aegina

Q109316963.bio: author of a history of Cyprus

Q109410243.bio: epic poet, author of a lost Hymn to Glaucus

Q109411255.bio: ancient author of a lost work on Athens

Q109567661.bio: Baeton was a man of ancient Macedonia who lived in the 4th century BCE. He was a contemporary of Alexander the Great, and participated in his campaigns, with his colleague Diognetus, as a bematist or "road engineer", that is, someone who measures distances in his marches.

Q10973743.bio: Astydamas was a tragic poet of ancient Greece who lived around the turn of 4th century BCE, from roughly 423 to 363 BCE. He is very often confounded in ancient sources with his more well known and successful son Astydamas the Younger, who was also a tragic poet.

Q1098296.bio: Saint Apollinaris Claudius, otherwise Apollinaris of Hierapolis or Apollinaris the Apologist, was a Christian leader and writer of the 2nd century.

Q109929283.bio: ancient author of a description of Arabia

Q11023957.bio: Heliodorus was a surgeon of the pneumatic school in the 1st century CE. He was probably from Egypt, and was mentioned in the Satires of Juvenal. Heliodorus wrote several books on medical technique which have survived in fragments and in the works of Oreibasius.

Q110263698.bio: paraphrases of works by Nicander and Oppian are attributed to him

Q1108102.bio: Chaeremon was an Athenian dramatist of the first half of the fourth century BCE. He was generally considered a tragic poet like Choerilus. Aristotle said his works were intended for reading, not for representation.

Q1108149.bio: Chionides an Athenian comic poet of the 5th century BCE, contemporary of Magnes. The Suda says that Chionides flourished eight years before the Greco-Persian Wars, that is, 487 BCE. But Augustus Meineke thinks that Chionides flourished no earlier than 460 BCE.

Q111188716.bio: Pseudo-Ptolemy is a designation used for the authors of pseudepigrapha that appeared under the name of the astronomer and geographer Ptolemy. These are not authentic works of Ptolemy but were either forged in his name or were mistakenly taken to be his.

Q1113270.bio: Archedemus of Tarsus was a Stoic philosopher who flourished around 140 BCE. Two of his works: On the Voice and On Elements, are mentioned by Diogenes Laërtius.

Q1113661.bio: Clearchus (date unknown) was an Athenian comic poet of the ancient Greek New Comedy whose works Corinthioi, Kithardos, and Pandoros Athenaeus quotes in the Deipnosophistae.

Q1113778.bio: Cleophon was an Athenian tragic poet. The titles of ten of his plays are given by the Suda: Acteon, Amphiaraos, Achilles, The Bacchantes, Dexamenus, Erigone, Thyestes, Leucippus, Persis, and Telephus.

Q1113821.bio: Cleidemus was a Greek author, perhaps of the fifth or fourth century BCE but definitely later than the battle of Plataea in 479 BCE, who produced a lost Atthis, a local history of Athens dealing with the traditional origins of the city's law and institutions.

Q112072524.bio: Petosiris to Nechepso is a letter describing an ancient divination technique using numerology and a diagram. It is likely to be a pseudepigraph.

Q1120896.bio: Cratinus the Younger (4th century BCE) was a comic poet of the Middle Comedy, and was a contemporary of Plato and of Corydus. He flourished in the middle of 4th century BCE, and as late as 324 BCE.

Q112108485.bio: ancient Iambic poet quoted by Photius

Q1121221.bio: Criton of Pieria (Greek: Κρίτων Πιεριώτης, Πιερεύς; Latin Crito Pieriota, Pieriotes, Pierius, Pierensis) was a 2nd-century Greek historian.

Q11240778.bio: Greek epigrammatic poet during the reign of Hadrian

Q1128200.bio: Lasus of Hermione was a Greek lyric poet of the 6th century BCE from the city of Hermione in the Argolid. He is known to have been active at Athens under the reign of the Peisistratids.

Q1129405.bio: Lesbonax of Mytilene, a Greek sophist and rhetorician, flourished in the time of Roman emperor Augustus.

Q1131105.bio: Acesander wrote a history of Cyrene. Plutarch speaks of a work of his respecting Libya, which may possibly be the same work as the history of Cyrene.

Q11321589.bio: George Bardanes (Greek: Γεώργιος Βαρδάνης, died. ca.

Q113417.bio: Terpander, of Antissa in Lesbos, was a Greek poet and citharede who lived about the first half of the 7th century BCE. He was the father of Greek music and through it, of lyric poetry, although his own poetical compositions were few and in extremely simple rhythms.

Q11373.bio: Abu Ma‘shar al-Balkhi, Latinized as Albumasar, was an early Persian Muslim astrologer, thought to be the greatest astrologer of the Abbasid court in Baghdad.

Q1139629.bio: hypothetical Roman historian who was said to have lived in the 2nd century CE

Q114280.bio: Antipater of Sidon was an ancient Greek poet of the 2nd and 1st centuries BCE. Cicero mentions him living in Rome during the time of Quintus Lutatius Catulus, and calls him a brilliant epigrammist, sometimes too fond of imitation.

Q1150145.bio: Polemon of Ilium, also known as Polemon Periegetes, was an ancient Greek periegete, geographer, and antiquarian.

Q1159316.bio: Praxiphanes a Peripatetic philosopher, was a native of Mytilene, who lived a long time in Rhodes. He lived in the time of Demetrius Poliorcetes and Ptolemy I Soter, and was a pupil of Theophrastus, about 322 BCE.

Q116508.bio: Oppian, also known as Oppian of Anazarbus, of Corycus, or of Cilicia, was a 2nd-century Greco-Roman poet during the reign of the emperors Marcus Aurelius and Commodus, who composed the Halieutica, a five-book didactic epic on fishing.

Q1165497.bio: Marcian of Heraclea was a minor Greek geographer from Heraclea Pontica in Late Antiquity.

Q1165512.bio: Marcus Argentarius was a Greek epigrammatist.

Q116639.bio: Nikephoros I was a Byzantine writer and Ecumenical Patriarch of Constantinople from 12 April 806 to 13 March 815.

Q117176.bio: Thespis was a stage actor in Ancient Greece.

Q11724959.bio: George Lapithes (fl. 1340s) was a medieval Cypriot writer, scholar and landowner. Lapithes was a Greek Cypriot whose name is thought to have come from the town of Lapithos.

Q117253.bio: Demosthenes was a Greek statesman and orator in ancient Athens. His orations constitute a significant expression of contemporary Athenian intellectual prowess and provide insight into the politics and culture of ancient Greece during the 4th century BCE.

Q1173486.bio: David the Invincible or David the Philosopher was a Neoplatonic philosopher of the 6th century.

Q1175642.bio: tragic poet in the 5th century BCE

Q1175868.bio: Menander of Ephesus (Ancient Greek: Μένανδρος; fl. c.

Q1177360.bio: Thallus of Miletus, was an epigrammatic poet, five of whose epigrams are preserved in the Greek Anthology.

Q117753773.bio: ancient Greek historian active in the 1st century BCE

Q1178430.bio: Aelius Moeris (probably flourished in the 2nd century A.D.) was a Greek grammarian, surnamed Atticista.

Q1179257.bio: Morsimus or Morsimos was a tragic poet of the 5th century BCE, around 450 to 400 BCE, and the member of a large dynasty of tragic poets. None of his plays survive.

Q1180120.bio: Musaeus of Ephesus was an Ephesian epic poet attached to the court of the kings of Pergamon, who wrote a Perseis in ten books and also poems about Eumenes and Attalus I.

Q1185502.bio: Demetrius Lacon or Demetrius of Laconia was an Epicurean philosopher, and a disciple of Protarchus.

Q1186259.bio: John, called Anagnostes, was a Greek historian of the fifteenth century.

Q11876199.bio: author of Phoenicica, often identified with Publius Hordeonius Lollianus

Q1189157.bio: Nausiphanes was an ancient Greek atomist philosopher from Teos.

Q118992.bio: Menander (; Ancient Greek: Μένανδρος, romanized: Ménandros; c. 342/341 - c.

Q119009595.bio: pair of ancient Greek historians who wrote a work on Athens

Q11905336.bio: author of an ancient road measurement guide

Q11905573.bio: Andronicus was a poet of Roman Greece. Andronicus was a contemporary of the emperor Constantius II, around 360 CE.

Q11905762.bio: ancient Greek epigrammatist, probably Roman by birth

Q11906114.bio: Antigenes was a Greek historian, who probably lived in the late fourth century BCE. He seems to have written a historical work about Alexander the Great.

Q11906256.bio: Apollonides Orapius or Horapius was an ancient Greek writer who wrote a work on Egypt, entitled Semenuthi, and seems also to have composed other works on the history and religion of the Egyptians.

Q11906342.bio: Arabius Scholasticus was a writer of classical antiquity who was the author of seven epigrams in the Greek Anthology, most of which are upon works of art. He lived probably in the reign of Justinian.

Q11906402.bio: ancient Greek poet of Old Comedy

Q11906438.bio: Aretades of Cnidus was an ancient Greek historian from the city of Cnidus. He wrote a work on the history of Macedon in three books at least, and another on the history of various Greek islands in two books at least.

Q11906503.bio: Aristodemus of Thebes was a writer of ancient Greece who wrote a work on his native city titled On Thebes. This work is often referred to by ancient authors, and appears to have dealt mostly with the antiquities of Thebes.

Q11906521.bio: Aristodicus of Rhodes was the author of one or possibly two epigrams in the Greek Anthology, but little further is known about him. Most scholars believe these originally came from The Garland of Meleager of Gadara.

Q11906535.bio: Aristonymus was a comic playwright and contemporary of Aristophanes and Ameipsias. We know the titles of only two of his comedies, Theseus, and Helios Shivering, of which only a few fragments are extant.

Q11906540.bio: Aristotle of Chalcis in Euboea was a historical writer of ancient Greece. He is mentioned by the writer Harpocration as the author of a work on the islands of Euboea.

Q11906634.bio: Archelaus, a poet of ancient Greece, is called in ancient sources an Egyptian, and is believed to have been a native of a town in Egypt called Chersonesus, as he is also called "Chersonesita". He wrote epigrams, some of which are still extant in the Greek Anthology.

Q11906650.bio: Archimelus was a writer of ancient Greece who was the author of an epigram on the great ship of Hiero II of Syracuse, which appears to have been built about 220 BCE.

Q11906653.bio: Archytas of Amphissa was a Greek poet who was probably a contemporary of Euphorion of Chalcis, about 300 BCE, since it was a matter of doubt with the ancients themselves whether the epic poem Γέρανος (Geranos) was the work of Archytas or Euphorion.

Q11906660.bio: Archedicus was an Athenian comic poet of the New Comedy, who wrote, at the instigation of Timaeus, against Demochares, the nephew of Demosthenes, and supported Antipater and the Macedonian party. The titles of two of his plays are preserved, Διαμαρτάνων and Θησαυρός.

Q11906748.bio: Artemon, called "Melopoios", from his being a Melic poet, appears to have been a contemporary of the comic playwright Aristophanes. It is usually believed that he is the author of the two epigrams still extant in the Greek Anthology.

Q11906926.bio: Aspasius of Byblos was a sophist of Ancient Greece who according to the Suda was a contemporary of the sophists Adrianus and Aelius Aristides, and who consequently lived in the reign of the emperors Marcus Aurelius and Commodus, around 180 CE.

Q11908666.bio: Basilides of Scythopolis (fl. 150 CE) was a philosopher, probably a Stoic. According to the Chronicle of Jerome, he was one of the "illustrious" teachers of Marcus Aurelius.

Q11910960.bio: fictional author who is cited as a source in the Historia Augusta

Q11914092.bio: poet and olympic boxing victor, 4th century B.C.

Q11914103.bio: Cleopatra the Physician was a Greek medical writer and author of a manual entitled Cosmetics. Six fragments of her Cosmetics survive in quotation from later medical writers.

Q11914106.bio: ancient Greek poet, author of an Argonautica

Q11916242.bio: ancient Greek historian cited by pseudo-Plutarch

Q11916243.bio: Ctesicles was the author of a chronological work (Chronika or Chronoi), of which two fragments are preserved in Athenaeus.

Q11916477.bio: Daphitas or Daphidas of Telmessus was a Greek grammarian and epigrammatist known for his sharp and insulting manner of speech. He wrote against Homer, claiming that Homer lied in saying the Athenians fought at Troy.

Q11916542.bio: ancient Greek poet of Middle or New Comedy

Q11917225.bio: ancient Greek rhetorician from Sardis (1st century CE)

Q11917252.bio: ancient Greek grammarian and student of Tryphon

Q11917288.bio: Dios was an ancient Greek philosopher of uncertain date. Certain Pythagorean writings on aesthetics are ascribed to him.

Q11917291.bio: Dioscorides was a Greek epigrammatist of the Hellenistic period.

Q11917296.bio: Diotogenes was a Neopythagorean philosopher. He wrote a work On Piety, of which three fragments are preserved in Stobaeus, and another On Kingship, of which two considerable fragments are likewise extant in Stobaeus.

Q11917697.bio: ancient Greek author of treatise on fish

Q11917927.bio: Deinias of Argos was an ancient Greek philosopher and historian of the 3rd century BCE. In 252 BCE he joined with Aristotle the Dialectician in an attempt to overthrow the rule of the tyrant Abantidas of Sicyon.

Q11919710.bio: Scamon of Mytilene was an ancient Greek historian. He wrote a treatise entitled Περὶ Εὑρημάτων (alternatively translated as about "discoveries" or "inventions").

Q11921164.bio: Athenian poet of Old Comedy, from Sicily

Q11921281.bio: Greek tragic poet, nephew of the less known Euripides

Q11921785.bio: ancient Greek poet of New Comedy

Q11922087.bio: bishop of Carpasia in Cyprus (5th century)

Q11925495.bio: Hermodorus, an Ephesian who lived in the 4th century BCE, was an original member of Plato's Academy and was present at the death of Socrates.

Q11934454.bio: ancient Greek poet of Old Comedy

Q11936462.bio: Menecles of Barca was a Greek historian of the 2nd century BCE. None of his works survives complete, but some are known from fragments.

Q11936495.bio: ancient Greek poet of Middle Comedy

Q11938720.bio: Nicholas Artabasdos Rhabdas was an early-14th century Byzantine mathematician. Born in Smyrna, he occupied a position in imperial administration in Constantinople.

Q11938781.bio: Nicostratus was a Greek playwright of the Middle Comedy. He was said to be the youngest son of Aristophanes.

Q11939090.bio: Nicias of Miletus was an ancient Greek physician, poet and epigrammatist from Miletus. A confidant of Theocritus (see Idylls 11, 13 and 28), he devoted himself to poetry and eight epigrams ascribed to his name survive in a fragmentary state.

Q11942191.bio: ancient Greek historian who wrote on Lycia

Q11942248.bio: writer who accompanied Alexander the Great

Q11949851.bio: Synesius Scholasticus was a Greek poet of the 6th century, who is the author of an epigram preserved in the Greek Anthology on a statue of Hippocrates. He appears to have lived shortly before the destruction of Berytus by an earthquake in 551 CE.

Q11950679.bio: Greek historian 1st century BCE, author of a history of the Roman civil war

Q11951538.bio: Theognetus was an Ancient Greek comic poet of the 3rd century BCE.

Q11951806.bio: doctor of emperor Tiberius or Claudius

Q11951908.bio: Timostratus was an Ancient Greek comic poet, who was active in the early second century BCE. His son Ariston and his grandson Poses were also comic poets.

Q1208079.bio: Diadochos of Photiki was a fifth-century Christian ascetic whose works are included in the Philokalia.

Q120964328.bio: epic poet of Cyrene nephew of Callimachus

Q121027421.bio: Pseudo-Elias (fl. c. 600?), also called Pseudo-David, was the author of a set of lectures on logic written in Ancient Greek that form a commentary on Porphyry's Isagoge. The commentary, except for the first seven lectures, survives in a number of medieval manuscripts.

Q1213430.bio: ancient Greek historian and paradoxographer from Lesbos of the Hellenistic age

Q1215423.bio: Achmet, son of Seirim, the author of a work on the interpretation of dreams, the Great Book of Interpretation of Dreams, is probably not the same person as Abu Bekr Mohammed Ben Sirin, whose work on the same subject is still extant in Arabic in the Royal Library at Paris, and…

Q121550.bio: John Kaminiates was a Greek resident of Thessalonica when the city, then one of the largest in the Byzantine Empire, was besieged and sacked by a Saracen force led by Leo of Tripoli in 904.

Q1215711.bio: Lynceus of Samos, brother of the historian Duris of Samos, was a classical Greek author of comedies, letters and humorous anecdotes. He lived in the late 4th and early 3rd centuries BCE and was a pupil of Theophrastus.

Q1218135.bio: ancient Greek poet of New Comedy

Q1221653.bio: Nymphis, son of Xenagoras, a native of Heraclea Pontica, lived in the middle of the third century BCE, and was a person of distinction in his native land, as well as a historical writer of some note.

Q1225578.bio: Orion of Thebes was a 5th-century grammarian of Thebes (Egypt), the teacher of Proclus the neo-Platonist, and of Aelia Eudocia, the wife of Emperor Theodosius II. He taught at Alexandria, Caesarea in Cappadocia and Constantinople.

Q1226821.bio: Diogenianus was a Greek grammarian from Heraclea in Pontus (or in Caria) who flourished during the reign of Hadrian (117-138).

Q1226977.bio: Greek epic poet, author of Bassarica

Q1226985.bio: Dionysius Scytobrachion (Scytobrachion meaning 'leather arm'), also known as Dionysius of Mytilene (the capital of Lesbos), was the author of a series of stories set in the region now known as Libya.

Q1226993.bio: Dionysius Periegetes, also known as Dionysius of Alexandria or Dionysius the African, was the author of a description of the then-known world in Greek hexameter verse. He is believed to have been from Alexandria and to have lived around the time of Hadrian (r.

Q122818293.bio: Philaretus was a medical writer to whom a version of De pulsibus ad Antonium, a Greek treatise on the pulse is attributed. His name is associated only with a Byzantine revision of the text, probably from the ninth century CE.

Q12282412.bio: 14th-century Orthodox Christian clergyman, writer, and hesychast

Q1228764.bio: Pamphos Ancient Greek Πάμφως (Pamphos) is an Athenian poet, allegedly a contemporary of Linus of Thrace, inventor of the ialémos. Two purported short fragments of his poems survive.

Q1229019.bio: Pancrates of Arcadia was a Greek poet of antiquity born in Arcadia, author of a poem on fishing entitled Halieuticus or Labours of the Sea. Three fragments are preserved in Athenaeus' Deipnosophistae.

Q1230889.bio: Mnaseas of Patrae or of Patara, whether that in Lycia or perhaps the Patara in Cappadocia was a Greek historian of the late 3rd century BCE, who is reckoned to have been a pupil in Alexandria of Eratosthenes.

Q123147.bio: Ammonius Hermiae was a Greek philosopher from Alexandria, Byzantine Egypt. A Neoplatonist, he was the son of the philosophers Hermias and Aedesia, the brother of Heliodorus of Alexandria and the grandson of Syrianus.

Q1231472.bio: Philostratus the Younger, also known as Philostratus of Lemnos, was a Greek sophist of the Roman imperial period.

Q1231696.bio: Paxamus, or Paxamos, was an ancient Greek author from the Hellenistic period. He composed a cookbook titled On Cooking and an agricultural textbook titled On Farming.

Q1233081.bio: Peisander of Camirus in Rhodes, Ancient Greek epic poet, supposed to have flourished about 640 BCE.

Q1234536.bio: Colotes of Lampsacus was a pupil of Epicurus.

Q1234615.bio: Phalaecus was an Ancient Greek lyric and epigrammatic poet, from whom the meter called Phalaecian took its name. He is occasionally referred to by the grammarians, but they give no information respecting his works, except that he composed hymns to Hermes.

Q1234872.bio: Philiscus of Miletus was an ancient Greek rhetoric teacher in the 4th century BCE and a student of Isocrates. Before his involvement in rhetoric, he was a renowned flutist ("most paradoxical") and for this reason, Isocrates called him "flute hole".

Q1234881.bio: Philiscus of Corcyra, or Philicus, was a distinguished tragic poet, and one of the seven who formed the Tragic Pleiad, was also a priest of Dionysus, and in that character he was present at the coronation procession of Ptolemy II Philadelphus in 284 BCE.

Q1234940.bio: Philoxenus of Alexandria was an Ancient Greek linguist ("grammarian") who lived and worked in Alexandria.

Q1235326.bio: Sosicrates of Rhodes was a Greek historical writer.

Q1235541.bio: Hermippus was the one-eyed Athenian writer of the Old Comedy, who flourished during the Peloponnesian War.

Q1236122.bio: Diphilus, of Sinope, was a poet of the new Attic comedy and a contemporary of Menander (342-291 BCE). He is frequently listed together with Menander and Philemon, considered the three greatest poets of New Comedy.

Q1236440.bio: Bion of Abdera (c. 430 - 370 BCE) (Greek: Βίων ὁ Ἀβδηρίτης, gen.

Q1236554.bio: Mago (Punic: 𐤌𐤂‬𐤍‬, mgn) was a Carthaginian writer, author of an agricultural manual in Punic which was a record of the farming knowledge of Carthage. The Punic text has been lost, but some fragments of Greek and Latin translations survive.

Q1238588.bio: Domninus of Larissa was an ancient Hellenistic Syrian mathematician.

Q123915878.bio: set of scholarly comments from Roman times found in some manuscripts of Homer's Iliad

Q1240239.bio: Theophilos Corydalleus was a Greek Neo-Aristotelian philosopher who initiated the philosophical movement known as Korydalism or Corydalism.

Q1240680.bio: ancient Greek musician and lyric poet

Q1241343.bio: Justus of Tiberias (Tiberias, c. 35 CE - Galilee, c. 100 CE) was a 1st century Jewish author and historiographer.

Q1243502.bio: Pythius, also known as Pytheos or Pythis, was a Greek architect, architecture theorist, and sculptor of the 4th century BCE.

Q1243832.bio: Roman poet who wrote in Greek

Q1247079.bio: Pamphilus of Alexandria was a Greek grammarian, of the school of Aristarchus of Samothrace.

Q1247278.bio: Theophylact was a Byzantine Archbishop of Ohrid and commentator on the Bible. He is regarded as a saint in the Eastern Orthodox Church, commemorated on December 31st.

Q12506564.bio: The Bibliotheca is a compendium of Greek myths and heroic legends, genealogical tables and histories arranged in three books, generally dated to the first or second century CE.

Q125247.bio: Cratylus was an ancient Athenian philosopher from the mid-late 5th century BCE, known mostly through his portrayal in Plato's dialogue Cratylus. He was a radical proponent of Heraclitean philosophy and influenced the young Plato.

Q1254602.bio: Chion was the son of Matris, a noble citizen of Heraclea, city on the coast of Bithynia in Asia Minor, and was a disciple of Plato.

Q1254612.bio: Nicochares was an Athenian poet of the Old Comedy, son of the comic playwright Philonides and contemporary with Aristophanes.

Q125551.bio: Parmenides of Elea was a pre-Socratic Greek philosopher from Elea in Magna Graecia (Southern Italy).

Q125855765.bio: ancient Greek poet of New Comedy

Q1266046.bio: Eutychius of Constantinople, considered a saint in the Catholic Church and Eastern Orthodox Christian traditions, was the patriarch of Constantinople from 552 to 565 and from 577 to 582.

Q1266186.bio: Theodosius of Bithynia was a Hellenistic astronomer and mathematician from Bithynia who wrote the Spherics, a treatise about spherical geometry, as well as several other books on mathematics and astronomy, of which two survive, On Habitations and On Days and Nights.

Q1271013.bio: Adrianus of Tyre, also written as Hadrian and Hadrianos, was a sophist of ancient Athens who flourished under the emperors Marcus Aurelius and Commodus.

Q1272693.bio: Kekaumenos is the family name of the otherwise unidentified Byzantine author of the Strategikon, a manual on military and household affairs composed c. 1078.

Q1273142.bio: Sisinnius II of Constantinople became Ecumenical Patriarch of Constantinople in 996 and held the post until his death in 998.

Q1273151.bio: Anthony III Stoudites was a Greek monk member of the Monastery of Stoudios (founded 462), and the Ecumenical Patriarch of Constantinople from 973 to 978. He died in Constantinople in 983.

Q12757084.bio: Paphnutius the Ascetic, also known as Paphnutius the Hermit, was an Egyptian anchorite of the fourth century. He is most famous for his accounts of the lives of many hermits of the Egyptian desert, such as Saint Onuphrius.

Q1277383.bio: Serapion of Antioch was a Patriarch of Antioch. He is known primarily through his theological writings, although all but a few fragments of his works have perished.

Q1279413.bio: Cercidas was a poet, Cynic philosopher, and legislator for his native city Megalopolis.

Q1280294.bio: The Alcmeonis is a lost early Greek epic which is considered to have formed part of the Theban cycle. There are only seven references to the Alcmeonis in ancient literature, and all of them make it clear that the authorship of the epic was unknown.

Q1283712.bio: Demetrios Chomatenos or Chomatianos, Eastern Orthodox Archbishop of Ohrid from 1216 to 1236, was a Byzantine priest and judge. His comprehensive legal education allowed him to exert substantial influence as judge, arbiter, confessor and advisor to the Byzantine imperial house.

Q128538.bio: Luke the Evangelist was one of the Four Evangelists-the four traditionally ascribed authors of the canonical gospels. The Early Church Fathers ascribed to him authorship of both the Gospel of Luke and the Acts of the Apostles.

Q12874624.bio: Besantinus was a Greek epigrammatist of the Roman period who flourished in Hadrian's era and was possibly from Rhodes.

Q12876261.bio: Diogenes of Athens was a writer of Greek tragedy in the late 5th or early 4th century BCE. His works are listed by the Suda as Semele, Achilles, Helen, Herakles, Thyestes, Medea, Oedipus, and Chrysippus.

Q12877300.bio: Erycius of Cyzicus was an Ancient Greek poet.

Q12878321.bio: John Diakrinomenos was a Byzantine ecclesiastical historian of the early 6th century. His nickname refers to his theology: he was one of the "hesitants" (diakrinomenoi) who rejected the Council of Chalcedon.

Q12881703.bio: Neophytos Rodinos was a 17th-century Greek Cypriot scholar and Catholic missionary. Born in Ottoman Cyprus, he later converted from Eastern Orthodoxy to Catholicism and undertook missionary work preaching in Italy, Poland, Greece, Turkey and Albania.

Q12881887.bio: Niccolò Sagundino (1402 - March 1464) was a Greek-born Venetian secretary, diplomat and humanist. He wrote numerous letters, as well as religious and philosophical treatises, mostly in Latin.

Q12901192.bio: Nessos of Chios was a pre-Socratic ancient Greek philosopher from the island of Chios.

Q1294734.bio: Tryphon or Trypho was a Greek grammarian who lived and worked in Alexandria.

Q1295215.bio: Satyrus of Callatis was a distinguished Peripatetic philosopher and historian, whose biographies of famous people are frequently referred to by Diogenes Laërtius and Athenaeus. He came from Callatis Pontica, as was learned from a Herculaneum papyrus.

Q129772.bio: Xenophon of Athens was a Greek military leader, philosopher, and historian. At the age of 30, he was elected as one of the leaders of the retreating Greek mercenaries, the Ten Thousand, who had been part of Cyrus the Younger's attempt to seize control of the Achaemenid Empire.

Q130650.bio: Philip II of Macedon was the king (basileus) of Macedon from 359 BCE until his death in 336 BCE.

Q1320139.bio: Theophilus Antecessor was a Byzantine jurist, translator from Latin to Greek and teacher.

Q1320609.bio: Hephaestion, Hephaistion, or Hephaistio of Thebes was a Hellenized Egyptian astrologer of late Antiquity (born CE 380) who wrote a Greek treatise known as the Apotelesmatics or Apotelesmatika around CE 415.

Q132157.bio: Zeno of Elea was a pre-Socratic Greek philosopher from Elea, in Southern Italy (Magna Graecia). He was a student of Parmenides and one of the Eleatics.

Q133337.bio: Solon was an archaic Athenian statesman, lawmaker, political philosopher (philosopher in an etymological sense), and poet. He was one of the Seven Sages of Greece and is credited with laying the foundations for Athenian democracy.

Q134588.bio: Pope Nicholas V, born Tommaso Parentucelli, was head of the Catholic Church and ruler of the Papal States from 6 March 1447 until his death in March 1455.

Q1347202.bio: Epiphanes was reputedly the author of On Righteousness, a notable early Gnostic literary work that promotes early socialist principles, that was quoted and discussed by Clement of Alexandria, in Stromaties, III. Epiphanes was also attributed with founding Monadic Gnosis. G.R.S.

Q1349817.bio: Castor of Rhodes, also known as Castor of Massalia or Castor of Galatia according to the Suda, or as Castor the Annalist, was a Greek grammarian and rhetorician. He was surnamed Philoromaeus and is usually believed to have lived about the time of Cicero and Julius Caesar.

Q1362371.bio: Pratinas was one of the early tragic poets who flourished at Athens at the beginning of the fifth century BCE, and whose combined efforts were thought by critics to have brought the art to its perfection.

Q1362779.bio: Michael Apostolius or Apostolius Paroemiographus, i.e. Apostolius the proverb-writer, was a Greek teacher, writer and copyist who lived in the fifteenth century.

Q1366567.bio: Philo the Dialectician was a Greek philosopher of the Megarian (Dialectical) school.

Q1370568.bio: Thibron was a Spartan general. He was sent out as harmost in 400 BCE, with an army of about 5,000 men, composed of 1,000 Neodamodes (emancipated helots) and 4,000 other Peleponesians, to aid the Ionians against Tissaphernes, who wished to bring them into subjection.

Q137152.bio: Aeneas of Gaza was a Neo-Platonic philosopher and a convert to Christianity who flourished towards the end of the fifth century.

Q1371938.bio: Tryphiodorus was an epic poet from Panopolis (today Akhmim), Egypt.

Q1379677.bio: Theophanes of Mytilene was an intellectual and historian from the town of Mytilene on the island of Lesbos who lived in the middle of the 1st century BCE. He was a friend of Pompey and wrote an adulatory history of the latter's expedition to Asia.

Q138368.bio: Euthymius Zigabenus or Zigadenus or Zygadenus was a 12th-century monk and commentator on the Bible. He was a friend of the Byzantine emperor Alexius I Comnenus, for whom he wrote a lengthy work on heresies, Panoplia Dogmatica or Panoply of Doctrine (or "Full Armour of Belief").

Q1383804.bio: Heracleides (or Heraclides) of Cyme is a little-attested Greek historian who wrote a multivolume Persica, or history of Persia, not extant.

Q138531.bio: Phlegon of Tralles was a Greek writer and freedman of the emperor Hadrian, who lived in the 2nd century CE.

Q1385977.bio: Ezekiel the Tragedian was an Egyptian actor who wrote in Alexandria. Naomi Yavneh dated his work to the 3rd century BCE, while Howard Jacobson estimates the 2nd century BCE. Evidence of the date is not definitive.

Q138664.bio: Philoxenus of Cythera was a Greek dithyrambic poet, an exponent of the "New Music".

Q1389145.bio: John the Lydian or John Lydus (CE 491 - c. 565) was a Byzantine administrator and writer.

Q140188.bio: Aristarchus of Samos was an ancient Greek astronomer and mathematician who presented the first known heliocentric model that placed the Sun at the center of the universe, with the Earth revolving around the Sun once a year and rotating about its axis once a day.

Q1405.bio: Augustus, also known as Octavian, was the founder of the Roman Empire and the first Roman emperor from 27 BCE until his death in CE 14.

Q1407.bio: Tiberius Julius Caesar Augustus was the second Roman emperor from CE 14 until his death, reigning as the second ruler of the Julio-Claudian dynasty. He succeeded his stepfather Augustus, the first Roman emperor.

Q1411.bio: Tiberius Claudius Caesar Augustus Germanicus, or simply Claudius, was a Roman emperor, ruling from CE 41 until his death in CE 54.

Q1413.bio: Nero was Roman emperor from 54 CE until his suicide in 68 CE, as the final emperor of the Julio-Claudian dynasty. Nero was born at Antium in CE 37, the son of Gnaeus Domitius Ahenobarbus and Agrippina the Younger (great-granddaughter of the emperor Augustus).

Q1421.bio: Titus Flavius Vespasianus was Roman emperor from 79 to 81 CE. A member of the Flavian dynasty, Titus succeeded his father Vespasian upon his death, becoming the first Roman emperor ever to succeed his biological father.

Q1425.bio: Trajan was a Roman emperor from CE 98 to 117, remembered as the second of the Five Good Emperors of the Nerva-Antonine dynasty.

Q1427.bio: Hadrian was Roman emperor from 117 to 138. His form of address as Roman emperor was Imperator Caesar Traianus Hadrianus Augustus.

Q142999.bio: Eusebius of Caesarea (c. CE 260/265 - 30 May CE 339), also known as Eusebius Pamphilius, was a historian of Christianity, exegete, and Christian polemicist from the Roman province of Syria Palaestina. In about CE 314 he became the bishop of Caesarea Palaestina.

Q1430.bio: Marcus Aurelius Antoninus was Roman emperor from 161 to 180 and a Stoic philosopher.

Q1435921.bio: late Roman historian whose works are lost

Q1449914.bio: Magnes was an Athenian comic poet of the 5th century BCE. Magnes and his contemporary Chionides are the earliest comic poets for whom victories are recorded in the literary competition of the Dionysia festival.

Q145090.bio: Zaleucus was the Greek lawgiver of Epizephyrian Locris, in Magna Graecia.

Q1453173.bio: Macedonius of Thessalonica or Macedonius Consul was a Byzantine hypatos during the reign of Justinian, and the author of 42 epigrams in the Greek Anthology, the best of which are some delicate and fanciful amatory pieces.

Q1458645.bio: Symmachus was a writer who translated the Hebrew Bible into Greek.

Q1465859.bio: Xenagoras was a Greek historian from Heraclea Pontica quoted by Dionysius of Halicarnassus, from whom we learn that Xenagoras wrote that Odysseus and Circe had three sons, Rhomos, Anteias, and Ardeas, who founded the three cities which were called by their names.

Q1487010.bio: Ptolemy Chennus or Chennos ("quail"), was an Alexandrine grammarian during the reigns of Trajan and Hadrian. According to the Suda, he was the author of an historical drama named Sphinx, of an epic, Anthomeros, in 24 books (both lost) and a Strange History.

Q1493398.bio: Simon of Athens was an Athenian writer on horses and horsemanship of the fifth century BCE. He is the earliest known ancient Greek writer on the subject; Pliny described him as primus de equitatu scripsit, "the first to have written on riding".

Q1496242.bio: Callinicus, surnamed or nicknamed Sutorius or Suetorius, sometimes known as Kallinikos of Petra or Callinicus of Petra was an ancient Greek historian of Arab descent, orator, rhetorician and sophist who flourished in the 3rd century.

Q14981671.bio: Oros of Alexander was a late classical/Byzantine lexicographer and grammarian active in the mid-5th century. According to the Suda he was born in Alexandria and taught in Constantinople.

Q1499216.bio: The Anonymus Cyzicenus is the anonymous author of an ecclesiastical history of the 5th century. It has often been misattributed to Gelasius of Cyzicus, an error going back to Photius and followed by the editor of the editio princeps.

Q15078686.bio: The name Antiphon the Sophist is used to refer to the writer of several Sophistic treatises. He probably lived in Athens in the last two decades of the 5th century BCE, but almost nothing is known of his life.

Q1519411.bio: John Chortasmenos was a Byzantine monk and bishop of Selymbria, who was a distinguished bibliophile, writer, and teacher.

Q1520934.bio: The Telegony is a lost epic poem of Ancient Greek literature. It is named after Telegonus, the son of Odysseus by Circe, whose name ("born far away") is indicative of his birth on Aeaea, far from Odysseus' home of Ithaca.

Q152221.bio: Philotheos Kokkinos was the Ecumenical Patriarch of Constantinople for two periods from August 1353 to December 1354 and from 8 October 1364 to August 1376, and a leader of the Byzantine monastic and religious revival in the 14th century.

Q153258.bio: Christophoros of Mytilene was a Greek-language poet living in the first half of the 11th century, born in Constantinople.

Q1541.bio: Marcus Tullius Cicero was a Roman statesman, lawyer, scholar, philosopher, orator, and writer who tried to uphold optimate principles during the political crises of the Roman Republic that led to the establishment of the Roman Empire.

Q1559544.bio: Flavian I of Antioch was a Patriarch of Antioch from 381 until his death. He was born about 320, most probably in Antioch.

Q15633815.bio: Julianus, or Julian, surnamed the Egyptian was a Greek Byzantine administrator and epigrammatist.

Q1563743.bio: Limenius was an Athenian composer of paeans and prosodia. As creator of the Second Delphic Hymn in 128 BCE, he is the earliest known composer in recorded history for a surviving piece of music, or one of the two earliest, or the second-earliest, depending first on whether one…

Q156600.bio: Anatolius of Constantinople was a Patriarch of Constantinople (November 449 - 3 July 458). He is regarded as a saint, by both the Orthodox and Catholic Churches.

Q15695299.bio: Platonius is the author of two writings on Greek comedy, which have been preserved in excerpts: On the Characteristics of Comedies and On the Characteristics of Styles, which today form part of the collection Prolegomena de comoedia. The time of his life is unknown;

Q15914510.bio: Troilus of Constantinople was a sophist from Side in Pamphylia of the late 4th and early 5th century. He taught in Constantinople.

Q1592862.bio: Sosylus of Lacedaemon was a Greek historian in the 3rd century BCE. He would campaign alongside Hannibal throughout the Second Punic War, teaching him Greek and recording the events of his campaign.

Q159905.bio: Hipparchus was a Greek astronomer, geographer, and mathematician. He is considered the founder of trigonometry, but is most famous for his incidental discovery of the precession of the equinoxes.

Q1613489.bio: Hermias was a Neoplatonic philosopher who was born in Alexandria.

Q1613558.bio: Hermesianax of Colophon was an Ancient Greek elegiac poet of the Hellenistic period, said to be a pupil of Philitas of Cos; the dates of his life and work are all but lost, but Philitas is supposed to have been born c. 340 BCE.
