Q361405.bio: Theodore the Studite, also known as Theodorus Studita and Saint Theodore of Stoudios/Studium, was a Byzantine Greek monk and abbot of the Stoudios Monastery in Constantinople.

Q3615044.bio: Ananius was a Greek iambic poet, contemporary with Hipponax (about 540 BCE). The invention of the satyric iambic verse called Scazon is ascribed to him as well as to Hipponax.

Q3615069.bio: Anaxicrates was a Greek writer of uncertain date, one of whose statements is compared with one of Cleitodemus. He wrote a work on Argolis.

Q3615071.bio: Anaxippus was an Athenian comic poet of the New Comedy, who was contemporary with Antigonus and Demetrius Poliorcetes, and flourished about 303 BCE. We have the titles of four of his plays, and perhaps of one more.

Q3616354.bio: Andromachus was the name of two Greek physicians, father and son, who lived in the time of Nero. Andromachus the Elder, was born in Crete, and was physician to Nero, 54-68 CE.

Q3616656.bio: Amphicrates of Athens was a sophist and rhetorician (of the Asiatic school).

Q3618433.bio: Antenor was a Greek writer of uncertain date, wrote a work upon the history of Crete, which on account of its excellence was called Delta, inasmuch as, says Ptolemy Hephaestion, the Cretans called that which is good Delton.

Q3618675.bio: Antidotus was an Athenian comic poet, of whom we know nothing, except that he was of the Middle Comedy period, which is evident from the fact that a certain play, the Homoia, is ascribed both to him and to the poet Alexis.

Q3618703.bio: ancient Greek author who wrote a work on chronology

Q3620703.bio: Apollophanes of Athens was a poet of the old Attic comedy. He appears to have been a contemporary of Strattis, and to have consequently lived about Olympiad 95.

Q3620704.bio: Apollonides of Smyrna was an epigrammatic poet of ancient Greece, who lived in the time of the Roman emperors Augustus and Tiberius.

Q3620706.bio: Apollonides was a tragic poet of ancient Greece, concerning whom nothing is known. He may have lived in the third century BCE. Two fragments of his dramas (TrGF 152) are preserved by Clement of Alexandria and Stobaeus.

Q3621469.bio: Archebulus or Archeboulus of Thera (or possibly Thebes, Greece) was a lyric poet who appears to have lived around the year 280 BCE, as Euphorion of Chalcis is said to have been instructed by him in poetry.

Q3621481.bio: Archemachus or Archemacchus was an ancient Greek writer who wrote on his native island (Euboea). His works consisted of at least three books.

Q3622659.bio: Aristias, son of Pratinas, was a dramatic poet of ancient Greece whose tomb Pausanias saw at Phlius, and whose satyric dramas, with those of his father, were considered to be surpassed only by those of Aeschylus.

Q3622711.bio: Aristonicus of Alexandria was a distinguished Greek grammarian who lived during the reigns of Augustus and Tiberius, contemporary with Strabo. He taught at Rome, and wrote commentaries and grammatical treatises.

Q3623149.bio: Harmodius of Lepreon was an ancient Greek writer, whose time is unknown. His work is repeatedly quoted by Athenaeus.

Q3623745.bio: Arrianus was a poet of ancient Greece who, according to the Suda, made a Greek translation in hexameter verse of Virgil's Georgics, and wrote an epic poem on the exploits of Alexander the Great, as well as a poem on Attalus I.

Q3624183.bio: Artemidorus of Tarsus was a grammarian of ancient Greece who lived around the 1st century BCE. He is mentioned by the geographer Strabo as one of the most distinguished persons of Tarsus.

Q3624209.bio: Artemon of Cassandreia was an ancient Macedonian grammarian, who seems to have lived after 316 BCE. He is mentioned by Athenaeus as the author of the following works: 1.

Q3624211.bio: Artemon of Pergamon was a rhetorician of ancient Greece, a grammarian and writer who wrote a history of Sicily, which is now lost.

Q3624868.bio: Asclepiades of Myrlea was a Greek grammarian, historian and astronomer disciple of Apollonius of Rhodes born in Myrlea (Bithynia) that lived in the 2nd and 1st centuries BCE. At the time of Pompey he was a teacher in Rome.

Q3624870.bio: Asclepiades was a writer of ancient Egypt who possessed, according to the Suda, a profound knowledge of Ancient Egyptian religion, and wrote hymns on his native gods.

Q3625041.bio: Aelius Antipater or Antipater of Hierapolis was a Greek sophist and rhetorician.

Q362589.bio: Leo the Deacon was a Byzantine Greek historian and chronicler. He was born around 950 at Kaloe in Asia Minor, and was educated in Constantinople, where he became a deacon in the imperial palace.

Q3627896.bio: Athenaeus was an epigrammatic poet whose work was mentioned by the historian Diogenes Laërtius. He was the author of two epigrams in the Greek Anthology.

Q3627898.bio: Athenion was a poet of Ancient Greek comedy. The Greek grammarian Athenaeus preserves an extensive extract from one of his plays, The Samothracians, in which a chef discourses philosophically about the role cooking plays in civilized society, namely that it "lured early humans…

Q3629160.bio: The Acts of Barnabas is a non-canonical pseudepigraphical Christian work that claims to identify its author as John Mark, the companion of Paul the Apostle, as if writing an account of Barnabas, the Cypriot Jew who was a member of the earliest church of Jerusalem;

Q3629529.bio: Augeas or Augias was an Athenian poet of the middle comedy who lived around the 4th or 5th century BCE.

Q36303.bio: Thales of Miletus was an Ancient Greek pre-Socratic philosopher from Miletus in Ionia, Asia Minor. Thales was one of the Seven Sages, founding figures of Ancient Greece.

Q3630469.bio: Autocrates was an Ancient Athenian poet of the old comedy. One of his plays is mentioned by the Suda and Aelian.

Q3633198.bio: Balagrus was a Greek writer of uncertain date, who wrote a work on the kingdom of Macedonia in two books at least.

Q363394.bio: Artavasdes II, also known as Artavazd II, was king of Armenia from 55 BCE to 34 BCE. A member of the Artaxiad dynasty, he was the son and successor of Tigranes the Great (r. 95-55 BCE), who ascended the throne of a still powerful and independent state.

Q363468.bio: Publius Herennius Dexippus, Greek historian, statesman and general, was an hereditary priest of the Eleusinian family of the Kerykes, and held the offices of archon basileus and eponymous in Athens.

Q3635627.bio: Basilis was a writer (or possibly multiple writers) of ancient Greece. Several ancient authors describe a writer named "Basilis" who wrote on geographical subjects, and it is generally assumed these are all the same person.

Q3636219.bio: Baton was an Athenian comic poet of the New Comedy, who flourished about 280 BCE. We have fragments of the following comedies by him: The Aetolian(s) The Euergetes Audrophonos Deceiving Together His plays appear to have been chiefly designed to ridicule the philosophers of the…

Q3636221.bio: Baton of Sinope was an ancient Greek historian and grammarian of the Hellenistic period.

Q363818.bio: Nicander of Colophon was a Greek poet, physician, and grammarian.

Q3640496.bio: Biton of Pergamon was an ancient Greek writer and engineer, who lived in the second or third century BCE. Only two of his works are known: a lost book on optics, entitled Optics, and an extant short treatise on siege machines, Construction of War Machines and Catapults.

Q364379.bio: Horapollo (from Horus Apollo; Ancient Greek: Ὡραπόλλων; fl. c.

Q365097.bio: Isaeus was one of the ten Attic orators according to the Alexandrian canon.

Q365110.bio: Philo of Larissa was a Greek philosopher. It is very probable that his actual name was "Philio." He was a pupil of Clitomachus, whom he succeeded as head of the Academy.

Q365183.bio: Themistius, nicknamed Euphrades, was a statesman, rhetorician and philosopher.

Q365678.bio: Evagrius Scholasticus was a Syrian scholar and intellectual living in the 6th century CE, and an aide to the patriarch Gregory of Antioch.

Q365927.bio: Pope Peter I of Alexandria was the 17th Pope and Patriarch of Alexandria from 302 to 311. He is revered as a saint by the Coptic Orthodox Church, the Eastern Orthodox Church, and the Catholic Church.

Q365941.bio: Theophilus of Alexandria was the 23rd Pope of Alexandria and Patriarch of the See of Saint Mark from 385 to 412.

Q365950.bio: Cleobulus was a Greek poet and a native of Lindos.

Q365977.bio: Bias of Priene was a Greek sage. He is widely accepted as one of the Seven Sages of Greece and spent his life working as a legal advocate free of charge for those who had been wronged.

Q366382.bio: George Syncellus was a Byzantine chronicler and ecclesiastical official. He lived many years in Palestine (probably in the Old Lavra of Saint Chariton or Souka, near Tekoa) as a monk, before coming to Constantinople, where he was appointed synkellos (literally, "cell-mate") to…

Q3667201.bio: Choerilus of Iasus was an epic poet of Iasus in Caria, who lived in the 4th century BCE. He accompanied Alexander the Great on his campaigns as court-poet.

Q367298.bio: Timaeus of Tauromenium was an ancient Greek historian. He was widely regarded by ancient authors as the most influential historian between the time of Ephorus (4th century BCE) and Polybius (2nd century BCE).

Q367377.bio: Hipponax, of Ephesus and later Clazomenae, was an Ancient Greek iambic poet who composed verses depicting the vulgar side of life in Ionian society.

Q367438.bio: Euthymenes of Massalia was a Greek explorer from Massalia (modern Marseille), who explored the coast of West Africa as far, apparently, as a great river, of which the outflow made the sea at its mouth fresh or brackish.

Q367946.bio: Apollinaris the Younger, also known as Apollinaris of Laodicea and Apollinarius, was a bishop of Laodicea in Syria. He is best known as a noted opponent of Arianism.

Q369129.bio: Dexippus was a Greek Neoplatonic philosopher from the 4th century CE, whose wrote a commentary on the Categories of Aristotle which is partially extant. Dexippus was likely a pupil of the Neoplatonist Iamblichus, but little else in known about his life.

Q3695456.bio: Constantine Akropolites, or Acropolites, was a Byzantine scholar and statesman in the fourteenth century.

Q370123.bio: Apollodorus of Artemita was a Greek historian who flourished between 130 and 87 BCE. He hailed from the Greco-Parthian city of Artemita in Apolloniatis and was a citizen of the Parthian Empire.

Q3705296.bio: Demetrius the Chronographer was a Jewish chronicler (historian) of the late 3rd century BCE, who lived probably in Alexandria and wrote in Greek.

Q37062.bio: John VIII Palaiologos was the penultimate Roman emperor to rule in Constantinople. Ruling from 1425 to 1448, he attempted to bring about the reunification of the Orthodox and Catholic churches and prioritised the protection of Constantinople against the Ottoman Empire.

Q37067.bio: Andronikos II Palaiologos, Latinized as Andronicus II Palaeologus, reigned as Byzantine emperor from 1282 to 1328. His reign marked the beginning of the recently restored empire's final decline.

Q37072.bio: John III Doukas Vatatzes, Latinized as Ducas Vatatzes, was Emperor of Nicaea from 1221 to 1254.

Q37082.bio: Theodore II Doukas Laskaris or Ducas Lascaris was Emperor of Nicaea from 1254 to 1258. He was the only child of Emperor John III Doukas Vatatzes and Empress Irene Laskarina.

Q37084.bio: John VI Kantakouzenos or Cantacuzene was a Byzantine emperor and nobleman, statesman, and general. He served as grand domestic under Andronikos III Palaiologos and regent for John V Palaiologos before reigning as Byzantine emperor in his own right from 1347 to 1354.

Q37097.bio: Manuel II Palaiologos or Palaeologus was Byzantine emperor from 1391 to 1425. Shortly before his death he was tonsured a monk and received the name Matthaios.

Q37142.bio: Constantine XI Dragases Palaiologos or Dragaš Palaeologus was the last reigning Byzantine emperor from 23 January 1449 until his death in battle at the fall of Constantinople on 29 May 1453.

Q372109.bio: Nicephorus Gregoras (; Greek: Νικηφόρος Γρηγορᾶς, Nikēphoros Grēgoras; c. 1295 - c.

Q372688.bio: Andrew of Crete, also known as Andrew of Jerusalem, was an 8th-century bishop, theologian, homilist, and hymnographer.

Q372763.bio: Eutyches or Eutyches of Constantinople was a presbyter and archimandrite at Constantinople.

Q373042.bio: Onasander or Onosander was a Greek philosopher.

Q3731015.bio: Heracleides of Sinope was a writer of ancient Greece. Under this name we possess a Greek epigram in the Greek Anthology.

Q373685.bio: Lycurgus (; Ancient Greek: Λυκοῦργος Λυκόφρονος Βουτάδης, romanized: Lykourgos Lykophronos Boutadēs; c. 390 - c.

Q3744914.bio: Philagathus, later known erroneously as Theophanes Cerameus, was a Greek monk and preacher from Sicily or Calabria.

Q3744959.bio: ancient Greek poet of New Comedy

Q375127.bio: Ecphantus or Ecphantos or Ephantus was an Ancient Greek pre-Socratic philosopher. He is identified as a Pythagorean of the 4th century BCE from Syracuse, Magna Graecia, but the details concerning his life are historically obscure;

Q3766483.bio: John Apokaukos was a Byzantine churchman and theologian. Having studied at Constantinople, he became bishop of Naupaktos and played a major role in the rivalry between the Epirote Church and the Ecumenical Patriarchate, exiled in the Empire of Nicaea.

Q377781.bio: Erasistratus (; Ancient Greek: Ἐρασίστρατος; c. 304 - c.

Q378236.bio: Aristides Quintilianus was the Greek author of an ancient musical treatise, Perì Musikês According to Theodore Karp, his three-volume work on music "constitutes one of the principal sources of modern knowledge of ancient Greek music and its relationship to other disciplines".

Q379987.bio: Geminus of Rhodes was a Greek astronomer and mathematician, who flourished in the 1st century BCE. An astronomy work of his, the Introduction to the Phenomena, survives; it was intended as an introductory astronomy book for students.

Q380453.bio: Dionysius the Younger, or Dionysius II, was a Greek politician who ruled Syracuse, Sicily from 367 BCE to 357 BCE and again from 346 BCE to 344 BCE.

Q380482.bio: Agathon was an Athenian tragic poet whose works have been lost. He is best known for his appearance in Plato's Symposium, which describes the banquet given to celebrate his obtaining a prize for his first tragedy at the Lenaia in 416.

Q380793.bio: Aelianus Tacticus, also known as Aelian (), was a Greek military writer who lived in Rome.

Q380826.bio: Aelius Herodianus or Herodian (fl. 2nd century CE) was one of the most celebrated grammarians of Greco-Roman antiquity.

Q380881.bio: Stephanus or Stephen of Byzantium was an Eastern Roman grammarian and the author of an important geographical dictionary entitled Ethnica. Only meagre fragments of the dictionary survive, but the epitome is extant, compiled by one Hermolaus, not otherwise identified.

Q380943.bio: Philostorgius was an Anomoean Church historian of the 4th and 5th centuries.

Q381048.bio: Stilpo or Stilpon (Ancient Greek: Στίλπων, Stílpōn; c. 360 - c.

Q381049.bio: Semonides of Amorgos was a Greek iambic and elegiac poet who is believed to have lived during the seventh century BCE.

Q381710.bio: Saint Symeon the New Theologian was an Eastern Orthodox monk and poet who was one of the three saints canonized by the Eastern Orthodox Church and given the title of "Theologian" (along with John the Apostle and Gregory of Nazianzus).

Q381874.bio: Gaius Musonius Rufus was a Roman Stoic philosopher of the 1st century CE. He taught philosophy in Rome during the reign of Nero and so was sent into exile in 65 CE, returning to Rome only under Galba.

Q381956.bio: Aëtius of Amida was a Byzantine Greek physician and medical writer, particularly distinguished by the extent of his erudition.

Q382785.bio: Corax was one of the founders (along with Tisias) of ancient Greek rhetoric.

Q383003.bio: Nikephoros Bryennios was a Byzantine general, statesman and historian. He was born at Orestias (Adrianople) in the theme of Macedonia.

Q3842153.bio: Machon was a playwright of the New Comedy.

Q384263.bio: Barlaam of Seminara or Barlaam of Calabria was a Basilian monk, theologian and humanistic scholar born in southern Italy.

Q3851977.bio: Matron of Pitane was an Ancient Greek poet and parodist.

Q3854645.bio: Menecrates of Syracuse, Magna Graecia, was the physician at the court of Philip of Macedon, 359-336 BCE. He seems to have been a successful practitioner but to have made himself ridiculous by calling himself Zeus and assuming divine honors.

Q3876106.bio: Nicophon, the son of a certain Theron, was an Athenian comic poet, a contemporary of Aristophanes in his later years. Athenaeus states that he belonged to Old Comedy, but it is more likely that he belonged to Middle Comedy.

Q388333.bio: Cadmus of Miletus was according to some ancient authorities, the oldest of the logographi. Scholars who accept this view, assign him to about 550 BCE; others regard him as purely mythical.

Q389558.bio: Tiberius Claudius Balbillus Modestus (died June CE 79), more commonly known as Tiberius Claudius Balbilus, was a distinguished Ancient Roman scholar, politician and a court astrologer to the Roman emperors Claudius, Nero, and Vespasian.

Q3907308.bio: Polyphrasmon was a Greek tragic playwright. He won the City Dionysia for tragedy in or about 471 BCE, and came in third place in 467 BCE for a tragic trilogy based on the story of Lycurgus (Lykourgeia);

Q3907964.bio: Iophon was a Greek tragic poet, son of Sophocles, and brother to Ariston.

Q391202.bio: Agathangelos is the pseudonym of the author of a life of the first apostle of Armenia, Gregory the Illuminator, who died about 332.

Q391216.bio: Agatharchides or Agatharchus of Cnidus was a Greek historian and geographer (flourished 2nd century BCE).

Q391254.bio: Eumelus of Corinth, of the clan of the Bacchiadae, is a semi-legendary 8th century BCE Greek poet to whom were attributed several epic poems as well as a celebrated prosodion, the treasured processional anthem of Messenian independence that was performed on Delos.

Q391419.bio: Dorotheus of Gaza, Dorotheus the Archimandrite or Abba Dorotheus, was a Christian monk and abbot.

Q391654.bio: Andocides was a logographer (speech writer) in Ancient Greece.

Q3951632.bio: Theophilus Protospatharius was the author of several extant Greek medical works.

Q39576.bio: Ptolemy II Philadelphus was the pharaoh and basileus of the Ptolemaic Kingdom from 284 to 246 BCE.

Q39595.bio: Ptolemy IV Philopator was the fourth pharaoh of Ptolemaic Egypt from 221 to 204 BCE. Ptolemy IV was the son of Ptolemy III and Berenice II.

Q39602.bio: Ptolemy III Euergetes was the third pharaoh of the Ptolemaic dynasty in Egypt from 246 to 222 BCE. The Ptolemaic Kingdom reached the height of its military and economic power during his kingship, as initiated by his father Ptolemy II Philadelphus.

Q3963931.bio: Sophaenetus was one of the leaders of the Ten Thousand, an army of Greek mercenaries in the service of Cyrus the Younger, in 401-400 BCE. A native of Stymphalus, he was an older man when he recruited and led one thousand hoplites to join Cyrus.

Q3975908.bio: Strattis was an Athenian comic poet of the Old Comedy. According to the Suda, he flourished later than Callias Schoenion.

Q3983912.bio: Theodorus was a Christian biblical scholar of the mid-4th century CE. He was bishop of Heraclea in Thrace, being appointed some time between 328 and 334; he was an ally of Eusebius against the Athanasians.

Q3983959.bio: Theopompus was an Athenian poet of the Greek Old Comedy, the son of Theodectus or Theodorus. He produced 24 plays.

Q3991389.bio: Timachidas of Rhodes was an ancient Greek poet and grammarian from the island of Rhodes who lived in 2nd/1st century BCE.

Q405173.bio: Aelius Theon was an Alexandrian sophist and author of a collection of preliminary exercises (progymnasmata) for the training of orators. He probably lived and wrote in the mid to late 1st century CE and his treatise is the earliest treatment of these exercises.

Q405969.bio: Aeneas Tacticus was one of the earliest Greek writers on the art of war and is credited as the first author to provide a complete guide to securing military communications.

Q4072299.bio: Simon Atumano was the Bishop of Gerace in Calabria from 23 June 1348 until 1366 and the Latin Archbishop of Thebes thereafter until 1380.

Q40939.bio: Aeschylus was an ancient Greek tragedian, often described as the father of tragedy. Academic knowledge of the genre begins with his work, and understanding of earlier Greek tragedy is largely based on inferences made from reading his surviving plays.

Q409616.bio: Aeschines of Miletus was a contemporary of Cicero, and a distinguished orator in the Asiatic style of eloquence, which, according to Cicero, "rushes with an impetuous stream.

Q409647.bio: Aeschines of Sphettus (Ancient Greek: Αἰσχίνης Σφήττιος, c. 425 BCE - c.

Q41155.bio: Heraclitus was an ancient Greek pre-Socratic philosopher from the city of Ephesus, which was then part of the Persian Empire.

Q4134212.bio: Gaudentius was a Greek music theorist in Classical Antiquity. Nothing is known of his life or background, or when he lived, except what can be inferred from his sole surviving work, Εἰσαγωγὴ ἁρμονική (English: Harmonic Introduction), a treatise.

Q41523.bio: Plutarch was a Greek and later Roman Middle Platonist philosopher, historian, biographer, essayist, and priest at the Temple of Apollo in Delphi.

Q415483.bio: Acacius of Constantinople served as the patriarch of Constantinople from 472 to 489. He was practically the first prelate in the East and was renowned for his ambitious participation in the Chalcedonian controversy.

Q41592.bio: Basil I, nicknamed "the Macedonian", was Byzantine emperor from 867 to 886. Born to a peasant family in the theme of Macedonia, he rose to prominence in the imperial court after gaining the favour of Emperor Michael III, whose mistress he married on his emperor's orders.

Q41600.bio: Alexios I Komnenos, Latinized as Alexius I Comnenus, was Byzantine emperor from 1081 to 1118. After usurping the throne he was faced with a collapsing empire and constant warfare throughout his reign.

Q41608.bio: Constantine VII Porphyrogenitus was the fourth Byzantine emperor of the Macedonian dynasty, reigning from 6 June 913 to 9 November 959. He was the son of Emperor Leo VI and his fourth wife, Zoe Karbonopsina, and the nephew of his predecessor Alexander.

Q41610.bio: Manuel I Komnenos was a Byzantine emperor of the 12th century who reigned over a crucial turning point in the history of Byzantium and the Mediterranean.

Q41618.bio: Leo VI, also known as Leo the Wise, was Byzantine Emperor from 886 to 912. The second ruler of the Macedonian dynasty (although his parentage is unclear), he was very well read, leading to his epithet.

Q41625.bio: Nikephoros II Phokas, Latinized Nicephorus II Phocas, was Byzantine emperor from 963 to 969. His career, not uniformly successful in matters of statecraft or of war, nonetheless greatly contributed to the resurgence of the Byzantine Empire during the 10th century.

Q41643.bio: Isaac I Komnenos or Comnenus was Byzantine emperor from 1057 to 1059, the first reigning member of the Komnenian dynasty. The son of the general Manuel Erotikos Komnenos, he was orphaned at an early age, and was raised under the care of Emperor Basil II.

Q41683.bio: Thucydides was an Athenian historian and general. His History of the Peloponnesian War recounts the 5th century BCE war between Sparta and Athens until the year 411 BCE.

Q41866.bio: Justinian I, also known as Justinian the Great, was Roman emperor from 527 to 565. His reign was marked by the ambitious but only partly realized renovatio imperii ('restoration of the Empire').

Q41980.bio: Democritus was an Ancient Greek pre-Socratic philosopher from Abdera, primarily remembered today for his formulation of an atomic theory of the universe. Democritus wrote extensively on a wide variety of topics.

Q4202467.bio: John Eugenikos was a late Byzantine cleric and writer. He was the brother of Mark Eugenikos, and like him an ardent opponent of the Union of the Churches.

Q4223358.bio: Cleonides is the author of a Greek treatise on music theory titled Εἰσαγωγὴ ἁρμονική Eisagōgē harmonikē (Introduction to Harmonics).

Q423894.bio: Acusilaus, Acusilas, Acousileos, or Akousilaos of Argos, son of Cabas or Scabras, was a Greek logographer and mythographer who lived in the latter half of the 6th century BCE but whose work survives only in fragments and summaries of individual points.

Q42458.bio: Anaximander was a pre-Socratic Greek philosopher who lived in Miletus, a city of Ionia (in modern-day Turkey). He belonged to the Milesian school and learned the teachings of his master Thales.

Q428139.bio: George Choiroboskos, Latinized as Georgius Choeroboscus, was an early 9th-century Byzantine grammarian and deacon.

Q42887.bio: Clement of Rome, also known as Pope Clement I, was the Bishop of Rome in the late first century. He is considered to be the first of the Apostolic Fathers of the Church.

Q429744.bio: Philinus of Agrigentum (3rd-century BCE), Magna Graecia, was a historian who lived during the First Punic War, who is said to have written history from a pro-Carthaginian standpoint.

Q430051.bio: Ptolemy the Gnostic, was a disciple of the Gnostic teacher Valentinius and is known for the Letter to Flora, an epistle he wrote to a wealthy woman named Flora, herself not a Gnostic.

Q4318.bio: Theopompus (Ancient Greek: Θεόπομπος, Theópompos; c. 380 BCE - c.

Q43182.bio: Eratosthenes of Cyrene was an Ancient Greek polymath: a philosopher, scholar, mathematician, geographer, poet, astronomer, and music theorist.

Q43216.bio: Epicurus was an ancient Greek philosopher who founded the philosophical school of Epicureanism, which taught that management of one's desires, removal of unnecessary fears, friendship, and virtuous living led to a pleasant life and constant happiness, the highest good.

Q432578.bio: Aelius Promotus was an ancient physician of Alexandria, of whose personal history no particulars are known, and whose date is uncertain. He is supposed by Villoison to have lived after the time of Pompey the Great, that is, in the 1st century BCE.

Q432737.bio: Lycophron was a Hellenistic Greek tragic poet, grammarian, and commentator on comedy, to whom the poem Alexandra is attributed (perhaps falsely).

Q433408.bio: Pausanias was the Agiad King of Sparta; the son of Pleistoanax. He ruled Sparta from 445 BCE to 427 BCE and again from 409 BCE to 395 BCE. He was the leader of the faction in Sparta that opposed the imperialist policy conducted by Lysander.

Q43353.bio: Aristophanes was an Ancient Greek comic playwright from Athens. He wrote forty plays, of which eleven survive virtually complete.

Q433647.bio: George Sphrantzes, also Phrantzes or Phrantza, was a late Byzantine Greek historian and Imperial courtier.

Q433852.bio: Ephippus of Olynthus was an Ancient Greek historian of Alexander the Great. It is commonly believed, though no reason is assigned, that Ephippus lived about or shortly after the time of Alexander.

Q433919.bio: Phintys was a Pythagorean philosopher, probably from the third century BCE. She wrote a work on the correct behaviour of women, two extracts of which are preserved by Stobaeus. According to Stobaeus, Phintys was the daughter of Callicrates, who is otherwise unknown.

Q434203.bio: Diogenes of Babylon (also known as Diogenes of Seleucia; Ancient Greek: Διογένης Βαβυλώνιος; Latin: Diogenes Babylonius; c. 230 - c.

Q43423.bio: Aesop was a Greek fabulist and storyteller credited with a number of fables now collectively known as Aesop's Fables.

Q434567.bio: Chariton of Aphrodisias was the author of an ancient Greek novel probably titled Callirhoe (based on the subscription in the sole surviving manuscript).

Q434773.bio: Crantor of Soli was an Ancient Greek philosopher and member of the Old Academy who was the first philosopher to write commentaries on the works of Plato.

Q434811.bio: Herodas, or Herondas, was a Greek poet and the author of short humorous dramatic scenes in verse, probably written in Alexandria during the 3rd century BCE.

Q435274.bio: Hieronymus of Cardia was a Greek officer, administrator, and historian from Cardia in Thrace, active from the late fourth to the mid-third century BCE.

Q4354540.bio: Bacchius of Tanagra, was one of the earliest commentators on the writings of Hippocrates and was a native of Tanagra in Boeotia. He was a follower of Herophilos, and a contemporary of Philinus.

Q4355017.bio: Diyllus, probably the son of Phanodemus the Atthidographer (a chronicler of the local history of Athens and Attica), wrote a universal history of the years 357-296 BCE. His work seems to have been a continuation of Ephorus' history, and was itself continued by Psaon of Plataea.

Q435531.bio: Hipparchus was a member of the ruling class of Athens and one of the sons of Pisistratus.

Q43654.bio: Nikolaos of Otranto (c. 1155/60, Otranto - 9 February 1235), also known as Nektarios of Casole, was a Greek abbot and author.

Q436634.bio: Cassius Longinus was a Greek rhetorician and philosophical critic.

Q43706.bio: John Chrysostom was a Church Father who served as Archbishop of Constantinople. He is known for his preaching and public speaking, his Divine Liturgy of Saint John Chrysostom, and his ascetic sensibilities.

Q437869.bio: Evagrius Ponticus, also called Evagrius the Solitary (345-399 CE), was a Christian monk and ascetic from Heraclea, a city on the coast of Bithynia in Asia Minor.

Q43920.bio: Macarius of Egypt (c. 300 - 391) was an Egyptian Christian monk and grazer hermit.

Q439491.bio: Symeon or Simeon (died c. 1000), distinguished as Symeon Metaphrastes or Symeon the Metaphrast, was a Byzantine writer and official regarded as a saint in the Eastern Orthodox Church. His feast day is celebrated on 9 or 28 November.

Q44011.bio: Gregory of Nazianzus, also known as Saint Gregory the Theologian or Gregory Nazianzen, was an early Roman Christian theologian and prelate who served as Archbishop of Constantinople from 380 to 381.

Q44024.bio: Athanasius I of Alexandria (c. 296-298 - 2 May 373), also called Athanasius the Great, Athanasius the Confessor, or, among Coptic Christians, Athanasius the Apostolic, was a Christian theologian and the 20th patriarch of Alexandria (as Athanasius I).

Q44079.bio: Cyril of Alexandria was the Patriarch of Alexandria from 412 to 444.

Q441138.bio: Lucius Cornelius Alexander Polyhistor was a Greek scholar who was enslaved by the Romans during the Mithridatic War and taken to Rome as a tutor. After his release, he continued to live in Italy as a Roman citizen.

Q441460.bio: Meleager of Gadara was a poet and collector of epigrams.

Q44170.bio: Ignatius of Antioch, also known as Ignatius Theophorus, was an early Christian writer and the Patriarch of Antioch.

Q441786.bio: Julia Balbilla was a Roman noble woman and poet. Whilst in Thebes, touring Egypt as part of the imperial court of Hadrian, she inscribed three epigrams which have survived.

Q44233.bio: Hesiod was an Ancient Greek poet generally thought to have been active between 750 and 650 BCE, around the same time as Homer.

Q442449.bio: Publius Rutilius Rufus (c. 160 BCE - after 78 BCE) was a Roman politician, soldier, orator, and historian. He was consul in 105 BCE, with Gnaeus Mallius Maximus as his colleague.

Q44248.bio: Jerome, also known as Jerome of Stridon, was an early Christian priest, confessor, theologian, translator, and historian; he is commonly known as Saint Jerome.

Q44258.bio: Basil of Caesarea, also called Saint Basil the Great (330 - 1 or 2 January 379), was an early Christian prelate. He served as Bishop of Caesarea Mazaca in Cappadocia from 370 until his death in 379.

Q443510.bio: Hesychius of Alexandria was a Greek grammarian who, probably in the 5th or 6th century CE, compiled the richest lexicon of unusual and obscure Greek words that has survived, probably by absorbing the works of earlier lexicographers.

Q443765.bio: Antoninus Liberalis was an Ancient Greek mythographer who probably flourished in the late 2nd or early 3rd century CE.

Q443983.bio: Aulus Postumius Albinus was a statesman of the Roman Republic, notably consul in 151 BCE. He was also a historian and wrote the Annals in Greek. Apparently the son of Aulus Postumius Albinus Luscus, he was praetor in 155 BCE, and consul in 151 BCE with Lucius Licinius Lucullus.

Q444079.bio: Joannes Stobaeus, from Stobi in Macedonia, was the compiler of a valuable series of extracts from Greek authors.

Q4441106.bio: Aphthonius of Antioch (Greek: Ἀφθόνιος Ἀντιοχεὺς ὁ Σύρος; fl. c.

Q444459.bio: Alcidamas, of Elaea, in Aeolis, was a Greek sophist and rhetorician, who flourished in the 4th century BCE.

Q444595.bio: Perictione was the mother of the Greek philosopher Plato. She was a descendant of Solon, the Athenian lawgiver.

Q445029.bio: Quadratus of Athens was an early Christian apologist, traditionally regarded as a disciple of the Apostles and one of the Seventy Disciples.

Q445848.bio: Artemidorus Daldianus or Ephesius was a professional diviner and dream interpreter who lived in the 2nd century CE. He is known from an extant five-volume Greek work, the Oneirocritica or Oneirokritikon (English: The Interpretation of Dreams).

Q446098.bio: Plato was an Athenian comic poet and contemporary of Aristophanes. None of his plays survive intact, but the titles of thirty of them are known, including a Hyperbolus (c.

Q446595.bio: Soranus of Ephesus was a Greek physician.

Q4484276.bio: Philo of Tarsus in Cilicia was a physician and pharmacologist of ancient Greece. He probably lived in or before the first century CE, as the physician and medical writer Galen speaks of him as having lived sometime before his own age.

Q450311.bio: Alypius of Alexandria was a Greek writer on music who flourished in the 4th century CE. Of his works, only a small fragment has been preserved, under the title of Introduction to Music.

Q450585.bio: Philaenis of Samos was supposedly the author of a famous ancient sex manual. According to a surviving fragment of a treatise which claims to have been written by her, she was from Samos, and her father was called Ocymenes.

Q451390.bio: Autolycus of Pitane (Greek: Αὐτόλυκος ὁ Πιταναῖος; c. 360 - c.

Q451550.bio: Philodemus of Gadara was an Epicurean philosopher and poet.

Q452077.bio: Menippus of Gadara was a Cynic satirist.

Q452225.bio: Eunomius (died c. 393 CE), one of the leaders of the extreme or "anomoean" Arians, who are sometimes accordingly called Eunomians, was born at Dacora in Cappadocia or at Corniaspa in Pontus.

Q453311.bio: Scylax of Caryanda was a Greek explorer and writer of the Achaemenid Empire during the late 6th and early 5th centuries BCE. His writings are lost, though occasionally they are cited or quoted by later Greek and Roman authors.

Q453465.bio: Eustathius of Thessalonica was a Byzantine Greek scholar and Archbishop of Thessalonica and is a saint in the Eastern Orthodox Church.

Q453860.bio: Publius Cornelius Scipio Nasica (Nasica meaning "pointed nose") was a consul of ancient Rome in 191 BCE. He was a son of Gnaeus Cornelius Scipio Calvus.

Q455523.bio: Babrius, also known as Babrias or Gabrias, was the author of a collection of Greek fables, many of which are known today as Aesop's Fables.

Q456560.bio: Myia (; Ancient Greek: Μυῖα, literally "Fly"; fl. c.

Q456649.bio: Maximus of Tyre, also known as Cassius Maximus Tyrius, was a Greek rhetorician and philosopher who lived in the time of the Antonines and Commodus, and who belongs to the trend of the Second Sophistic.

Q458108.bio: Apion, also called Apion Pleistoneices and Apion Mochthos was an Egyptian grammarian and sophist in first century Egypt.

Q45936.bio: Strabo was a Greek geographer who lived in Asia Minor during the transitional period of the Roman Republic into the Roman Empire.

Q460766.bio: Ameipsias of Athens was an Ancient Greek comic poet, a contemporary of Aristophanes, whom he twice bested in the dramatic contests.

Q462992.bio: Apollonius Molon or Molo of Rhodes, was a Greek rhetorician. He was a native of Alabanda, a pupil of Menecles, and settled at Rhodes, where he opened a school of rhetoric.

Q463201.bio: Gennadius of Constantinople was the patriarch of Constantinople from August 458 until his death. Gennadius is known to have been a learned writer who followed the School of Antioch of literal exegesis, although few writings have been left about him.

Q463364.bio: Bion was an ancient Greek bucolic poet from Smyrna, probably active at the end of the second or beginning of the first century BCE. He is named in the Suda as one of three canonical bucolic poets alongside Theocritus and Moschus.

Q463564.bio: Xenophon of Ephesus was a Greek writer.

Q4673235.bio: Acestodorus was a Greek historical writer who is cited by Plutarch, and whose work contained, as it appears, an account of the Battle of Salamis among other things. The time at which he lived is unknown.

Q4688536.bio: Aeschylus of Alexandria was an epic poet who must have lived before the end of the 2nd century, and whom Athenaeus calls a well-informed man. One of his poems bore the title Amphitryon, and another Messeniaca.

Q470689.bio: John Kinnamos or Joannes Kinnamos or John Cinnamus, was a Byzantine historian. He was imperial secretary to Emperor Manuel I (1143-1180), whom he accompanied on his campaigns in Europe and Asia Minor.

Q471464.bio: Asclepiades of Samos (Sicelidas) was an ancient Greek epigrammatist and lyric poet who flourished around 270 BCE. He was a friend of Hedylus and possibly of Theocritus.

Q471916.bio: Hecataeus of Abdera (Greek: Ἑκαταῖος ὁ Ἀβδηρίτης; c. 360 BCE - c.

Q4720496.bio: Alexander of Athens was a comic poet, the son of Aristion, whose name occurs in an inscription given in Böckh, who refers it to the 145th Olympiad in 200 BCE.

Q4721014.bio: Alexandrides of Delphi was an ancient Greek historian of uncertain date. If we may judge from the subjects on which his history is quoted as an authority, it would seem that his work was a history of Delphi.

Q4721241.bio: Alexarchus or Alexarch was an ancient Greek historian, who wrote a work on the history of Italy, of which Plutarch quotes the third book.

Q472620.bio: Artemidorus of Ephesus was a Greek geographer, who flourished around 100 BCE. His work in eleven books is often quoted by Strabo. What is thought to be a possible fragment of his work is considered by some scholars to be a forgery.

Q472809.bio: Apollonius Dyscolus is considered one of the greatest of the Greek grammarians.

Q473291.bio: Anastasius Sinaita, also called Anastasius of Sinai or Anastasius the Sinaite, was a Greek writer, priest and abbot of Saint Catherine's Monastery on Mount Sinai.

Q473381.bio: Ammonius of Athens, sometimes called Ammonius the Peripatetic, was a philosopher who taught in Athens in the 1st century CE. He was a teacher of Plutarch, who praises his great learning, and introduces him discoursing on religion and sacred rites.

Q473421.bio: Dinarchus or Dinarch (Greek: Δείναρχος; Corinth, c. 361 - c.

Q474586.bio: Eusebius of Emesa was a learned Christian cleric of the Greek church, and a pupil of Eusebius of Caesarea. He was born in Edessa (in today's southeastern Turkey) and became the bishop of Emesa (in today's Syria).

Q474872.bio: Amphilochius of Iconium was a Christian bishop of the fourth century, son of a Cappadocian family of distinction, born, perhaps at Caesarea, ca. 339/340, died probably 394-403.

Q475001.bio: Dictys Cretensis, i.e. Dictys of Crete of Knossos was a legendary companion of Idomeneus during the Trojan War, and the purported author of a diary of its events, that deployed some of the same materials worked up by Homer for the Iliad.

Q4780405.bio: Apollonius Paradoxographus was the otherwise unknown author of a paradoxographical work entitled Mirabilia or Historiae Mirabiles. This was compiled from the works of earlier writers around the 2nd century BCE. Nothing is known about Apollonius.

Q4784288.bio: Araros, son of Aristophanes, born in 387 BCE, was an Athenian comic poet of the Middle Comedy. His brothers Philippus and Nicostratus were also comic poets.

Q4813242.bio: Athanasios of Emesa was a Byzantine jurist living in the 6th century. Coming from the first generation of jurists to practice after Justinian completed the codification of Roman law, he worked as a teacher of law, rhetor and advocate.

Q4813402.bio: Athenaeus of Attalia (1st century CE), was a physician, and the founder of the Pneumatic school of medicine. He was born in Cilicia, at Attalia according to Galen, or at Tarsus according to Caelius Aurelianus.

Q48305.bio: Euripides was a Greek tragedian of classical Athens. Along with Aeschylus and Sophocles, he is one of the three authors of Greek tragedy for whom any plays have survived in full.

Q48735055.bio: Aretes of Dyrrachium was an ancient chronographer - that is, a natural philosopher whose work dealt with the construction of calendars. Some of his calculations were mentioned by the ancient Roman writer Censorinus, so we know Aretes lived in or before the 3rd century CE.

Q488577.bio: Anaxandrides was an Ancient Greek comic poet of the Middle Comedy. His father was Anaxander.

Q4891141.bio: Theodotus of Ancyra was a fifth-century bishop of Ancyra (modern Ankara). He was a theologian who attended the Council of Ephesus in 431, during the reign of Byzantine Emperor Theodosius II.

Q4896406.bio: Carytius of Pergamum was an ancient Greek grammarian who lived at the end of the 2nd century BCE, all of whose works are now lost. Among his works were Historical Notes, On the Dramatic Poets, and On Sotades.

Q48998226.bio: Archinus was a historian of ancient Greece, who lived at an uncertain date, and who wrote a work on the history of Thessaly. This book, however, is now lost.

Q48998607.bio: Architimus was a writer of ancient Greece. His date is uncertain, but was some time before the 1st century CE. We know him to have written a work about the greek region Arcadia.

Q4966577.bio: Alexis was a Greek comic poet of the Middle Comedy period.

Q503075.bio: Crates of Mallus was a Greek grammarian and Stoic philosopher, leader of the literary school and head of the library of Pergamum. He was described as the Crates from Mallus to distinguish him from other philosophers by the same name.

Q504744.bio: Hellanicus (or Hellanikos) of Lesbos, also called Hellanicus of Mytilene (Greek: Ἑλλάνικος ὁ Μυτιληναῖος, Hellánikos ho Mutilēnaîos; c. 490 - c.

Q504771.bio: Philo of Byblos, also known as Herennius Philon, was an antiquarian writer of grammatical, lexical and historical works in Greek. He is chiefly known for his Phoenician history assembled from the writings of Sanchuniathon.

Q505931.bio: Aretaeus is one of the most celebrated of the ancient Greek physicians. Little is known of his life.

Q5063276.bio: Cephalion was a Roman historian of the time of Hadrian. He wrote a History of Assyria from the time of Ninus and Semiramis to that of Alexander the Great.

Q506540.bio: Didymus Chalcenterus (Latin; Greek: Δίδυμος Χαλκέντερος, Dídymos Chalkénteros, "Didymus Bronze-Guts"; c. 63 BCE - c.

Q506553.bio: Olympiodorus of Thebes (Ancient Greek: Ὀλυμπιόδωρος ὁ Θηβαῖος; born c. 380, fl.

Q506564.bio: Nicholas Kabasilas or Cabasilas was a Byzantine mystic and theological writer. Kabasilas is revered as a saint within the Eastern Orthodox Church.

Q506789.bio: Melanippides of Melos, one of the most celebrated lyric poets in the use of dithyramb, and an exponent of the "new music."

Q507036.bio: Lucius Annaeus Cornutus was a Stoic philosopher who flourished in the reign of Nero, when his house in Rome was a school of philosophy.

Q5092559.bio: Chersias of Orchomenus (fl. late 7th century BCE) was an archaic Greek epic poet whose work is all but lost today.

Q510209.bio: Sannyrion was an Athenian comic poet of the late 5th century BCE, and a contemporary of Diocles and Philyllius, according to the Suda. He belonged to the later years of Old Comedy and the start of Middle Comedy.

Q510659.bio: Choricius of Gaza was a Gaza-based Greek sophist and rhetorician of Late Antiquity. With writings dating to the early sixth century, he flourished in the time of Anastasius I (CE 491-518) as a scholar and public orator.

Q510719.bio: Eutocius of Ascalon (; Greek: Εὐτόκιος ὁ Ἀσκαλωνίτης; c. 480s - c.

Q510737.bio: Lucian of Antioch, known as Lucian the Martyr, was a Christian presbyter, theologian, and martyr.

Q511971.bio: Eustathius of Antioch, sometimes surnamed the Great, was a Christian patriarch of Antioch in the 4th century. His feast day in the Eastern Orthodox Church, Syriac Orthodox Church and Coptic Orthodox Church is February 21 (Amshir 27 in the Coptic calendar).

Q512691.bio: Sophron of Syracuse, Magna Graecia, was a writer of mimes.

Q513793.bio: Andronikos Doukas Kamateros was a Byzantine aristocrat, senior official under Emperor Manuel I Komnenos, and theologian, best known for his theological treatise Sacred Arsenal.

Q514262.bio: Androtion, was a Greek orator, and one of the leading politicians of his time. He was born between 415 and 405 BCE, the son of Andron, who was a member of the Four Hundred and an associate of Theramenes.

Q515249.bio: Caecilius of Calacte was a rhetorician and literary critic active in Rome during the reign of Augustus. The main source of information about Caecilius' life is the Suda, which says that he was from Sicily, originally called Archagathus, possibly of slave origins, and Jewish.

Q515542.bio: Agathemerus was a Greek geographer who during the Roman Greece period published a small two-part geographical work titled A Sketch of Geography in Epitome, addressed to his pupil Philon. The son of Orthon, Agathemerus is speculated to have lived in the 3rd century.

Q5163837.bio: Constantine Meliteniotes was a Greek ecclesiastical writer in the Byzantine Empire and a prominent supporter of the Union of Lyons between the Greek Orthodox Church and the Roman Catholic Church.

Q5163851.bio: Constantine Stilbes was a Byzantine rhetor and clergyman, and a prolific author of ecclesiastical treatises, letters, and poetry.

Q51672.bio: Herod I or Herod the Great (c. 72 - 4 or 1 BCE) was a Roman Jewish client king of the Herodian kingdom of Judea. He is known for his colossal building projects.

Q5173981.bio: Cosmas Vestitor (his nickname vestitor means "imperial wardrobe officer") was a Byzantine homiletic. He lived between 730 and 850 and left five sermons on the translation of the relics of St.

Q518300.bio: Methodius of Olympus (died c. 311) was an early Christian bishop, ecclesiastical author, and martyr.

Q518544.bio: Paul the Silentiary, also known as Paulus Silentiarius, was a Greek Byzantine poet and courtier to the emperor Justinian at Constantinople.

Q5185744.bio: Crinis was a Stoic philosopher who lived in the 2nd and 1st centuries BCE, who was contemporary with and likely a pupil of Archedemus of Tarsus.

Q5187254.bio: Crobylus is thought to be an Athenian Middle Comedy poet, although there is no specific ancient evidence to this effect. Crobylus is said to have lived sometime after 324 BCE. He is sometimes confused with Hegesippus.

Q51884.bio: John of Damascus or John Damascene, born Yūḥana ibn Manṣūr ibn Sarjūn, was a Christian monk, priest, hymnographer, and apologist. He was born and raised in Damascus c. CE 675 or CE 676;

Q519513.bio: Marcellus of Ancyra was a Bishop of Ancyra and one of the bishops present at the Council of Ancyra and the First Council of Nicaea.

Q520917.bio: Aristeas was a semi-legendary Greek poet and miracle-worker, a native of Proconnesus in Asia Minor, active ca. 7th century BCE. The Suda claims that, whenever he wished, his soul could leave his body and return again.

Q521203.bio: Duris of Samos (or Douris) was a Greek historian and was at some period tyrant of Samos. Duris was the author of a narrative history of events in Greece and especially Macedonia from 371 BCE to 281 BCE, which has been lost.

Q5252438.bio: Deimachus or Daimachus was a Greek from Plataeae, who lived during the third-century BCE. He became an ambassador to the court of the Mauryan ruler Bindusara "Amitragatha" (son of Chandragupta Maurya) in Pataliputra in India. Deimachus was sent by Antiochus I Soter.

Q525814.bio: Ptolemais of Cyrene was a music theorist, author of Pythagorean Principles of Music. She lived perhaps in the 3rd century BCE, and "certainly not after the first century CE." She is the only known female music theorist of antiquity.

Q5264.bio: Hippocrates of Kos, also known as Hippocrates II, named after his grandfather Hippocrates I (also Hippocrates of Kos or Hippocrates I of Kos) was a Greek physician and philosopher of the classical period who is considered one of the most outstanding figures in the history of…

Q529263.bio: George Hamartolos or Hamartolus was a Byzantine monk in Constantinople under Michael III (840-867) and the author of a chronicle of some importance.

Q530515.bio: John Tzetzes was a Byzantine poet and grammarian who lived at Constantinople in the 12th century. He is known for making significant contributions in preserving much valuable information from ancient Greek literature and scholarship.

Q531475.bio: Hicesius was a Greek physician, who probably lived at the end of the 1st century BCE, as he is quoted by Crito, and lived shortly before Strabo. He was a follower of Erasistratus, and was at the head of a celebrated medical school established at Smyrna.

Q531732.bio: Gregory II of Constantinople (born George of Cyprus; Greek: Γρηγόριος ὁ Κύπριος, romanized: Grēgorios ho Kyprios or Greek: Γεώργιος ὁ Κύπριος, romanized: Geōrgios ho Kyprios; c. 1241 - c.

Q5332381.bio: Echephyllides was an Ancient Greek grammarian or historian. He is mentioned by Stephanus of Byzantium, and by the scholia on Plato's Phaedo.

Q534163.bio: Xanthus of Lydia was a Greek historian, logographer and citizen of Lydia who, during the mid-fifth century BCE, wrote texts on the history of Lydia known as Lydiaca, a work which was highly commended by Dionysius of Halicarnassus. Xanthus also wrote occasionally about geology.

Q535769.bio: Metrodorus of Chios was a Greek philosopher, belonging to the school of Democritus, and an important forerunner of Epicurus.

Q5374757.bio: Empylus (1st century BCE) was an Ancient Roman rhetorician. He was the companion, as we are told by Plutarch, of Brutus, to whom he dedicated a short essay, not destitute of merit, on the death of Caesar.

Q537755.bio: Polyaenus or Polyenus ( POL-ee-EE-nəs; see ae (æ) vs. e; Ancient Greek: Πoλύαινoς, romanized: Polyainos, "much-praised") was a 2nd-century Roman Macedonian author and rhetorician, known best for his Stratagems in War, which has been preserved.

Q5382223.bio: Ephippus of Athens was an Ancient Greek comic poet of the middle comedy. We learn this from the testimonies of Suidas and Antiochus of Alexandria, and from the allusions in his fragments to Plato, and the Academic philosophers, and to Alexander of Pherae and his contemporaries,…

Q5382922.bio: Epigonus of Thessalonica (dates unknown) is an epigrammatist quoted in the Greek Anthology. Both the Palatine and Planudean codices attribute AP 9.261, an epigram on an ageing vine, to Epigonus; the Planudean codex attributes two more poems to him.

Q5383069.bio: Epinicus or Epinikos, was an Athenian comic poet of the New Comedy. Two of his plays are known, Hypoballomenai and Mnêsiptolemos.

Q539514.bio: Metrodorus of Lampsacus was a Pre-Socratic philosopher from the Greek town of Lampsacus on the eastern shore of the Hellespont.

Q539577.bio: Guarino Veronese or Guarino da Verona (1374 - 14 December 1460) was an Italian classical scholar, humanist, and translator of ancient Greek texts during the Renaissance. In the republics of Florence and Venice he studied under Manuel Chrysoloras (c.

Q540679.bio: Paul of Aegina or Paulus Aegineta was a 7th-century Byzantine Greek physician best known for writing the medical encyclopedia Medical Compendium in Seven Books. He is considered the “Father of Early Medical Writing”.

Q5414339.bio: Eustathios Rhomaios was a senior judge and writer on law of the Byzantine Empire.

Q541746.bio: Moero or Myro was a woman poet of the Hellenistic period from the city of Byzantium (modern Istanbul).

Q542808.bio: Hermarchus or Hermarch (Ancient Greek: Ἕρμαρχoς, Hermarkhos; c. 325 - c.

Q543629.bio: Hermias was an obscure Christian apologist, presumed to have lived in 3rd century. Nothing is known of him, except his name.

Q544378.bio: Dares Phrygius i.e Dares of Phrygia, according to Homer, was a Trojan priest of Hephaestus. He was later thought to have been the author of an account of the destruction of Troy.

Q544716.bio: Cineas was a Thessalian diplomat and historian who served as an important adviser of King Pyrrhus of Epirus.

Q544987.bio: Aristobulus of Cassandreia, Greek historian, son of Aristobulus, probably a Phocian settled in Cassandreia, accompanied Alexander the Great on his campaigns.

Q547681.bio: Philemon (Ancient Greek: Φιλήμων; c. 362 BCE - c.

Q5477015.bio: Leonidas of Alexandria was a Greek epigrammatist active at Rome during the reigns of Nero and Vespasian. Some of his epigrams are preserved in the Greek Anthology, and in one he lays claim to having invented the isopsephic epigram.

Q548104.bio: Julius Pollux was a Greek scholar and rhetorician from Naucratis, Roman Egypt.

Q549010.bio: Hephaestion was a grammarian of Alexandria who flourished in the age of the Antonines.

Q552447.bio: Nicholas I Mystikos or Mysticus was the Ecumenical Patriarch of Constantinople from 1 March 901 to 1 February 907 and from 15 May 912 to his death on 15 May 925. His feast day in the Eastern Orthodox Church is 16 May.

Q552759.bio: Parrhasius of Ephesus was a famed painter of Ancient Greece. Active during an era when other painters were starting to depict realistic scenes with shading, Parrhasius stood out by sticking to the older technique of line-drawing, and innovated new ways to portray volume using…

Q552862.bio: Philiscus of Aegina was a Cynic philosopher from Aegina, who lived in the latter half of the 4th century BCE.

Q554362.bio: Antigonus of Carystus, a Greek writer on various subjects, flourished in the 3rd century BCE. After some time spent at Athens and travelling, he was summoned to the court of Attalus I (241 BCE-197 BCE) of Pergamum.

Q557776.bio: Procopius of Gaza was a Christian sophist and rhetorician, one of the most important representatives of the Rhetorical School of Gaza.

Q558074.bio: Cyriacus of Ancona or Ciriaco de' Pizzicolli (31 July 1391 - 1452) was a humanist and antiquarian who came from a prominent family of merchants in Ancona, a maritime republic on the Adriatic coast of the Italian Peninsula.

Q559151.bio: Nossis was a Hellenistic poet from Epizephyrian Locris in Magna Graecia. Probably well-educated and from a noble family, Nossis was influenced by and claimed to rival Sappho.

Q559866.bio: Alciphron was an ancient Greek sophist, and the most eminent among the Greek epistolographers. Regarding his life or the age in which he lived we possess no direct information whatsoever.

Q560535.bio: George of Pisidia was a Byzantine poet, born in Pisidia. As an important early poet of Byzantine literature, he "contributed a great deal to the formation of many of the main features of Byzantine poetry".

Q561934.bio: Constantine Manasses was a Byzantine chronicler and poet who was active during the reign of Manuel I Komnenos (1143-1180). His main work was Synopsis Chronike, a poetic overview of world history.

Q563283.bio: Gaius Asinius Quadratus (fl. CE 248) was a Greek historian of Rome and Parthia of the third century.

Q5647936.bio: Neilos Doxapatres was a Byzantine Greek monk, theologian, and writer active in Constantinople and Sicily during the first half of the 12th century.

Q569024.bio: Polystratus; died 219/18 BCE) was an Epicurean philosopher, and head (scholarch) of the Epicurean school in Athens.

Q5697818.bio: Hedyle was an ancient Greek poet.

Q5701563.bio: Apollodorus of Tarsus was a tragic poet of ancient Greece, who is mentioned by Eudocia and in the Suda as having written six tragedies; only the titles of these plays have survived. Nothing further is known about him.

Q572956.bio: Antander was a man of Syracuse, Magna Graecia, of the 3rd and 4th centuries BCE. He was the older brother of Agathocles, king of Syracuse, and was a commander -- or strategos -- of the troops sent by the Syracusans to the relief of Crotona when it was besieged by the Bruttii…

Q5732548.bio: Heraclitus Paradoxographus is the author of the lesser-known of two works known as Peri Apiston (On Unbelievable Tales). Palaephatus was the author of a better-known work of paradoxography with the same title, mentioned more often in antiquity.

Q577769.bio: Antimachus of Colophon, or of Claros, was a Greek poet and grammarian, who flourished about 400 BCE.

Q577773.bio: Antimachus of Teos was an early Greek epic poet. According to Plutarch, he observed a solar eclipse in 753 BCE, the same year in which Rome was founded.

Q580565.bio: Palaephatus was the author of a rationalizing text on Greek mythology, the paradoxographical work On Incredible Things (Περὶ ἀπίστων; Incredibilia), which survives in a (probably corrupt) Byzantine edition.

Q580661.bio: Antiochus of Syracuse was a Greek historian of Magna Graecia, who flourished around 420 BCE. Little is known of Antiochus' life, but his works, of which only fragments remain, enjoyed a high reputation because of their accuracy.

Q581550.bio: Michael Glykas or Glycas was a 12th-century Byzantine historian, theologian, mathematician, astronomer and poet. He was probably from Corfu and lived in Constantinople.

Q581732.bio: Antipater of Tarsus was a Stoic philosopher. He was the pupil and successor of Diogenes of Babylon as leader of the Stoic school, and was the teacher of Panaetius.

Q581764.bio: Antipater of Thessalonica (Ancient Greek: Ἀντίπατρος ὁ Θεσσαλονικεύς; c. 10 BCE - c.

Q581833.bio: Marinus was a Byzantine Neoplatonic philosopher, mathematician and rhetorician born in Flavia Neapolis (modern Nablus), Palaestina Secunda.

Q584287.bio: Apelles was a second-century Gnostic Christian thinker. He began his ministry as a disciple of Marcion of Sinope, likely in Rome.

Q58559.bio: Pope Leo IX was the Bishop of Rome and ruler of the Papal States from 12 February 1049 to his death in 1054. Leo IX is considered to be one of the most historically significant popes of the Middle Ages;

Q585711.bio: Asclepiades of Tragilus was an ancient Greek literary critic and mythographer of the 4th century BCE, and a student of the Athenian orator Isocrates.

Q588467.bio: Themison of Laodicea was the founder of the Methodic school of medicine, and one of the most eminent physicians of his time.

Q59137.bio: Diogenes of Oenoanda was an Epicurean Greek from the 2nd century CE who carved a summary of the philosophy of Epicurus onto a portico wall in the ancient Greek city of Oenoanda in Lycia (modern day southwest Turkey).

Q59138.bio: Diogenes Laërtius was a biographer of the Greek philosophers. Little is definitively known about his life, but his surviving work, Lives and Opinions of Eminent Philosophers, remains a primary source for the history of ancient Greek philosophy.

Q59180.bio: Diogenes the Cynic, also known as Diogenes of Sinope, was an ancient Greek philosopher during the period of Classical Greece, and one of the founders of Cynicism.

Q596816.bio: Flavius Dioscorus lived during the 6th century CE in the village of Aphrodito, Egypt, and therefore is called by modern scholars Dioscorus of Aphrodito.

Q60125.bio: George Akropolites was a Byzantine historian and statesman, born in Constantinople.

Q601998.bio: Leontius of Byzantium was a Byzantine Christian monk and the author of an influential series of theological writings on sixth-century Christological controversies.

Q60461.bio: Arcadius of Antioch was a Greek grammarian who flourished in the 2nd century CE. According to the Suda, he wrote treatises on orthography and syntax, and an onomasticon (vocabulary), described as "a wonderful production." Περὶ τόνων (On Accents), an epitome of the major work of…

Q6057726.bio: Apollonius of Aphrodisias in Cilicia is described in the Suda as a high priest and a historian.

Q606249.bio: Antonius Diogenes was the author of an ancient Greek romance entitled The Wonders Beyond Thule. Scholars have placed him in the 2nd century A.D., but his age was unknown even to Photius I, Patriarch of Constantinople, who wrote a synopsis of the romance.

Q608224.bio: Creophylus is the name of a legendary early Greek epic poet, native to Samos or Chios. He was said to have been a contemporary of Homer and author of the lost epic Capture of Oechalia.

Q609147.bio: Phylarchus was a Greek historical writer whose works have been lost, but not before having been considerably used by other historians whose works have survived.

Q610433.bio: Antyllus was a Greek surgeon, who lived in the 2nd century CE in Rome. He is most notable for his method of treatment of aneurysms.

Q622258.bio: Alexander Numenius, or (according to the Suda) Alexander, son of Numenius, was a Greek rhetorician who flourished in the first half of the 2nd century. About his life almost nothing is known.

Q622261.bio: Alexander Aetolus or Alexander the Aetolian was a Hellenistic Greek poet and grammarian, who worked at the Library of Alexandria and composed poetry in a variety of genres, now almost entirely lost. He is the only known Aetolian poet of antiquity.

Q628384.bio: Metagenes was an Athenian comic poet of the Old Comedy, contemporary with Aristophanes, Phrynichus, and Plato. The Suda gives the following titles of his plays: Αὖραι, Μαμμάκυθος, Θουριοπέρσαι, Φιλοθύτης, Ὅμηρος ἢ Ἀσκηταί, some of which appear to be corrupt.

Q628944.bio: Apollodorus of Gela, Magna Graecia, in Sicily was a New Comedy playwright. According to Eudokia Makrembolitissa and the Suda, he was a contemporary of Menander, and accordingly lived between the years 340 and 290 BCE.

Q641051.bio: Arius Didymus was a Stoic philosopher and teacher of Augustus.

Q64466.bio: Agriopas was a writer of ancient Greece mentioned by Pliny the Elder. He was the author of an account of the Olympic victors, called the Olympionicae.

Q645774.bio: Bolus of Mendes was a philosopher, a neopythagorean writer of works of esoterica and medicine, in Ptolemaic Egypt.

Q649082.bio: Apsines of Gadara was a Greek rhetorician.

Q650448.bio: Manuel Moschopoulos, was a Byzantine commentator and grammarian, who lived during the end of the 13th and the beginning of the 14th century and was an important figure in the Palaiologan Renaissance. Moschopoulos means "little calf," and is probably a nickname.

Q651181.bio: Alcaeus of Messene was an ancient Greek poet, who flourished between 219 and 196 BCE. Twenty-two of his short poems or epigrams survive in the Greek Anthology, from some of which his date may be fixed at around the late 3rd/early 2nd century BCE.

Q6524970.bio: Leon of Pella or Leo the Egyptian (4th century BCE) was a historian, priest and theologian. He wrote the book On the Gods in Egypt, based on an apocryphal letter of Alexander the Great to his mother Olympias.

Q654760.bio: Lucillius was the author of one hundred twenty three epigrams in Greek preserved in the Greek Anthology.

Q658260.bio: Charon of Lampsacus was an Ionian historiographer active in the first half of the 5th century BCE, credited with regional histories, a Hellenica, local horoi (chronicles), chronographic lists, and a periplous - all lost and preserved only in fragments and testimonia.

Q660578.bio: Theodore I Palaiologos (or Palaeologus) (c. 1355 - 24 June 1407) was despot (despotēs) in the Morea from 1383 until his death on 24 June 1407.

Q662932.bio: Persaeus of Citium, son of Demetrius, was a Greek Stoic philosopher, and a friend and favourite student of Zeno of Citium.

Q664196.bio: Aristaenetus was an ancient Greek epistolographer who flourished in the 5th or 6th century. Under his name, two books of love stories, in the form of letters, are extant;

Q666209.bio: Theagenes of Rhegium was a Greek literary critic of the 6th century BCE from Rhegium (modern Reggio Calabria), in Magna Graecia.

Q666230.bio: Aristobulus of Alexandria also called Aristobulus the Peripatetic (fl. c. 181-124 BCE) and once believed to be Aristobulus of Paneas, was a Hellenistic Jewish philosopher of the Peripatetic school, though he also used Platonic and Pythagorean concepts.

Q666667.bio: Aristocles of Messene, in Sicily, was a Peripatetic philosopher, who probably lived in the 1st century CE.

Q6668972.bio: Lollius Bassus is the author of ten epigrams in the Greek Anthology. He is called, in the title of the second epigram, a native of Smyrna.

Q667361.bio: Aristophon was an Athenian comic poet of the Middle Comedy. He was probably victorious at least once at the Lenaia around 350 BCE (IG II2 2325.151).

Q668225.bio: Aristoxenus of Selinus (modern Selinunte in Sicily) was a poet of ancient Greece who is said to have been the first who wrote poetry in anapaestic meters.

Q6691.bio: Homer was an ancient Greek poet who is widely credited as the author of the Iliad and the Odyssey, two epic poems that are foundational works of ancient Greek literature.

Q669691.bio: Timotheus of Miletus was a Greek musician and dithyrambic poet, an exponent of the "new music." He added one or more strings to the lyre, whereby he incurred the displeasure of the Spartans and Athenians (E. Curtius, Hist of Greece, bk.

Q672126.bio: John VIII of Constantinople, a native of Trebizond, was a Byzantine intellectual, jurist, and Ecumenical Patriarch of Constantinople from 1064 to 1075.

Q6756392.bio: Marcellinus was the author of a Life of Thucydides, found in some of the ancient commentaries on the History of the Peloponnesian War by Thucydides.

Q6756482.bio: Marcellus of Side a native of Side in Pamphylia, was a physician born towards the end of the 1st century CE, and lived during the reigns of Hadrian and Antoninus Pius, 117-161 CE.

Q6758334.bio: Marcus Mettius Epaphroditus of Chaeroneia was an Ancient Greek grammarian of the 1st century.

Q679837.bio: Dionysius of Corinth, also known as Saint Dionysius, was the bishop of Corinth circa CE 171. His feast day is commemorated on April 8.

Q6812616.bio: Melissa (3rd century BCE) was a Pythagorean philosopher. Her name derives from the Greek word melli meaning honey.

Q681601.bio: Leo the Mathematician, the Grammarian or the Philosopher was a Byzantine philosopher and logician associated with the Macedonian Renaissance and the end of the Second Byzantine Iconoclasm. His only preserved writings are some notes contained in manuscripts of Plato's dialogues.

Q681878.bio: Aristarchus or Aristarch of Tegea was a Greek tragic poet and a contemporary of Sophocles and Euripides. He lived to be a centenarian, composed seventy plays, and won two tragic victories.

Q6835560.bio: Michael of Ephesus or Michael Ephesius was a Byzantine scholar.

Q68482.bio: Michael I of Constantinople was the Ecumenical Patriarch of Constantinople from 1043 to 1059.

Q686157.bio: Mesomedes of Crete was a Greek citharode and lyric poet and composer of the early 2nd century CE in Roman Greece. Prior to the discovery of the Seikilos epitaph in the late 19th century, the hymns of Mesomedes were the only surviving written music from the ancient world.

Q6915403.bio: Moschion, was an Athenian tragic poet. Nothing is known about his life; he probably lived in the second half of the 3rd century BCE. Three titles and a few fragments of his plays are preserved by Stobaeus.

Q695534.bio: Tyrannion was a Greek grammarian brought to Rome as a war captive and slave.

Q695923.bio: Ammonius Grammaticus was a 4th-century Egyptian priest. In 391, he was involved in a violent revolt centred at Alexandria's Serapeum, where the pagan rebels tortured and killed captured Christians.

Q696632.bio: Amphis was an Athenian comic poet of uncertain origin from approximately the 4th century BCE. Pollux seems to refer to Amphis as a Middle Comedy poet, and Amphis' own repeated references to the philosopher Plato place him in the early to mid-4th century BCE.

Q6981248.bio: Naumachius was a Greek didactic poet. Of his poems, seventy-three hexameters (in three fragments) are preserved by Stobaeus in his Florilegium (4.22b.32, 4.23.7, 4.32c.76).

Q6993672.bio: Neophytos of Cyprus, Saint Neophytos, Neophytos the Recluse was a Cypriot Orthodox monk, priest, and sometime hermit, whose writings preserved a history of the early crusades.

Q7025693.bio: Nicholas Kallikles was a prominent Greek physician and a leading court poet active in the Byzantine court in Constantinople during the reigns of Alexios I Komnenos (r. 1081-1118) and John II Komnenos (r. 1118-1143).

Q703544.bio: Hesychius of Miletus, Greek chronicler and biographer, surnamed Illustrius, son of an advocate, lived in Constantinople in the 6th century CE during the reign of Justinian.

Q704973.bio: Theodore II Palaiologos or Palaeologus (c. 1396 - 21 June 1448) was Despot in the Morea from 1407 to 1443 and in Selymbria from then until his death.

Q706089.bio: Artapanus of Alexandria was a historian, of Alexandrian Jewish origin, who is believed to have lived in Alexandria, during the later half of the 3rd or 2nd century BCE. Although most scholars assume Artapanus lived in Alexandria, others argue he resided in the countryside.

Q707344.bio: Numenius of Apamea was a Greek philosopher, who lived in Rome, and flourished during the latter half of the 2nd century CE. He was a Neopythagorean and forerunner of the Neoplatonists.

Q7091719.bio: Onatas was a Pythagorean philosopher who lived in or around the 5th century BCE, possibly in either Croton or Tarentum in Magna Graecia.

Q709305.bio: Conon was a Greek grammarian and mythographer of the age of Augustus (who lived 63 BCE - 14 CE), the author of a work titled Διηγήσεις (Narrations), addressed to Archelaus Philopator, king of Cappadocia.

Q712328.bio: Theodorus of Cyrene (Ancient Greek: Θεόδωρος ὁ Κυρηναῖος, romanized: Theódōros ho Kyrēnaîos; fl. c.

Q7124091.bio: Paeon of Amathus was an early Hellenistic historian from Amathus on the Island of Cyprus, mentioned in the writings of Plutarch and the lexicographer Hesychius of Alexandria.

Q712572.bio: Philistus, son of Archomenidas, was a Greek historian from Sicily.

Q7127720.bio: Palladius was a Greek medical writer, some of whose works are still extant.

Q712814.bio: Serapion of Alexandria was a physician who lived in the 3rd century BCE. He belonged to the Empiric school, and so much extended and improved the system of Philinus of Cos, that the creation of the school is attributed to him by some ancient writers.

Q7129426.bio: Pamphilus the Theologian was probably a late sixth century Palestinian compiler writing in the aftermath of the Council of Chalcedon and the fall-out this produced in the eastern Christian provinces.

Q713482.bio: Callistratus, Greek sophist and rhetorician, probably flourished in the 3rd (or possibly 4th) century CE. He wrote Ekphraseis, descriptions of fourteen works of art in stone or brass by distinguished artists.

Q713530.bio: Isidore of Pelusium was born in Egypt to a prominent Alexandrian family.

Q7145274.bio: George I served as Greek Patriarch of Alexandria between 621 and 631, succeeding St. John the Almsgiver.

Q714841.bio: Eustathius of Epiphania was a sixth-century Byzantine historian. Eustathius was born in Epiphania (modern Hama, Syria).

Q715478.bio: Diodorus Cronus was an Ancient Greek philosopher and dialectician connected to the Megarian school.

Q7155483.bio: Pseudo-Scymnus is the name given by Augustus Meineke to the unknown author of a work on geography written in Classical Greek, the Periodos to Nicomedes. It is an account of the world (periegesis) in 'comic' iambic trimeters which is dedicated to a King Nicomedes of Bithynia.

Q716355.bio: Alcetas was the brother of Perdiccas and the son of Orontes from Orestis. He is first mentioned as one of Alexander the Great's generals in his Indian expedition.

Q716416.bio: Hippo was a pre-Socratic Greek philosopher.

Q716811.bio: Hermogenes of Priene (late 3rd - early 2nd century BCE) was a Hellenistic architect, best known for designing a temple of Artemis Leukophryene (Artemision) at Magnesia in Lydia, an Ionian colony on the banks of the Maeander river in Anatolia.

Q718070.bio: Achaeus of Eretria was a Greek playwright and author of tragedies and satyr plays.

Q718142.bio: Servilius Damocrates was a Greek physician at Rome in the middle to late 1st century CE. He may have received the praenomen "Servillius" from his having become a client of the Servilia gens.

Q7181457.bio: Pherenicus was an epic poet from Heraclea Pontica. He treated of Metamorphoses and similar fabulous tales.

Q7184092.bio: Phillipos Monotropos or Philippus Solitarius ("Phillip the Recluse"; Ancient Greek: Φίλιππος ο Μονότροπος; fl. c.

Q7186007.bio: Philo was a Greek poet and writer. He was a Hellenistic Jewish author of an epic poem in Greek hexameters on the history of Jerusalem.

Q7186040.bio: Philocles, was an Athenian tragic poet during the 5th century BCE. Through his mother, Philopatho, he had three famous uncles: Aeschylus, the famous poet, Cynaegirus, hero of the battle of Marathon, and Ameinias, hero of the battle of Salamis.

Q719224.bio: Macarius Magnes, sometimes referred to as Macarius of Magnesia, is the author of a work of Christian apologetics contesting the writings of a Neo-Platonic philosopher. He was unknown for centuries until the discovery of a manuscript at Athens in 1867.

Q720494.bio: Herodorus of Heraclea was a native of Heraclea Pontica who wrote a history on Heracles around 400 BCE. Plutarch references Herodorus several times in his account of Theseus in Parallel Lives.

Q722430.bio: Philagrius of Epirus was a Greek medical writer from Epirus, who lived after Galen and before Oribasius, and therefore probably in the 3rd century CE. According to the Suda he was a pupil of a physician named Naumachius, and practiced his profession chiefly at Thessalonica.

Q722953.bio: Severian, Bishop of Gabala in Syria, was a popular preacher in Constantinople from around 400 until 404. He became the enemy of John Chrysostom and helped condemn him at the Synod of the Oak.

Q7234624.bio: Potamo or Potamon) of Mytilene in Lesbos, son of Lesbonax the rhetorician, was himself a rhetorician in the time of the Roman emperor Tiberius, whose favour he enjoyed. He is mentioned by Plutarch as an authority regarding Alexander the Great.

Q7235.bio: Sophocles was an ancient Greek tragedian, one of three from whom at least two plays have survived in full.

Q725225.bio: Thrasyllus of Mendes, also known as Thrasyllus of Alexandria and by his Roman name Tiberius Claudius Thrasyllus (fl. second half of the 1st century BCE and first half of the 1st century - died 36,), was a Greek Egyptian grammarian and literary commentator.

Q7254404.bio: A number of late 3rd-century Christian works are pseudepigraphically attributed to Dorotheus of Tyre. These works describe the lives of the Apostles and their disciples, including tradition about Barnabas living in Rome.

Q725712.bio: Leo Allatius (c. 1586 - January 1669) was a Greek scholar, theologian, and keeper of the Vatican Library.

Q725758.bio: Pherecydes of Leros was, according to the Suda, an ancient Greek historian from the island of Leros. He is said to have lived "before the seventy-fifth Olympiad" (480-477 BCE) and authored three works: On Leros, On Iphigenia, and On the Festivals of Dionysus.

Q7258134.bio: Publius Hordeonius Lollianus (2nd century CE) was a celebrated Greek sophist in the time of Hadrian and Antoninus Pius. Referred to as just Lollianus, by Philostratus, and the Suda, an Athenian Greek inscription, dating from c.

Q7263938.bio: Python of Catana, Magna Graecia, was a dramatic poet of the time of Alexander, whom he accompanied into Asia, and whose army he entertained with a satyric drama, called Agen when they were celebrating the Dionysia on the banks of the Hydaspes.

Q726892.bio: Menecrates of Ephesus was a Greek didactic poet of the Hellenistic period. Menecrates composed a poem titled Works, which was inspired by Hesiod's Works and Days, This poem also incorporated a discussion of bees, drawing from Aristotle's studies.

Q728059.bio: Musaeus of Athens was a legendary Greek polymath, philosopher, historian, prophet, seer, priest, poet, and musician, said to have been the founder of priestly poetry in Attica. He composed dedicatory and purificatory hymns and prose treatises, and oracular responses.

Q729109.bio: Parthenius of Nicaea or Myrlea in Bithynia was a Greek grammarian and poet. According to the Suda, he was the son of Heraclides and Eudora, or according to Hermippus of Berytus, his mother's name was Tetha.

Q729492.bio: Diodore of Tarsus was a Christian bishop, monastic reformer, and theologian.

Q72981031.bio: Quintus Sulpicius Maximus (81/82-94 CE) - was an ancient Roman boy poet, whose memorial contains the only known example of juvenilia from the ancient Roman world.

Q730625.bio: Asius of Samos was an ancient Greek poet whose work survives in the form of fragments quoted by other ancient authors. All that is known about the man is that he was from Samos and that his father's name was Amphiptolemus.

Q731078.bio: Secundus the Silent (fl. 2nd century CE) was a philosopher who lived in Athens in the early 2nd century, who had taken a vow of silence.

Q732098.bio: Asclepius of Tralles was a Neoplatonic philosopher and mathematician who was a student of Ammonius Hermiae.

Q732715.bio: Polycrates was a sophist from Athens, who later retired to the island of Cyprus. He wrote a work titled The Indictment of Socrates, thought to have been written during the 390s BCE.

Q733961.bio: Pope Peter III of Alexandria also known as Peter Mongus was the 27th Pope of Alexandria and Patriarch of the See of St. Mark.

Q73527.bio: Arcesilaus was a Greek Hellenistic philosopher. He was the founder of Academic Skepticism and what is variously called the Second or Middle or New Academy - the phase of the Platonic Academy in which it embraced philosophical skepticism.

Q736433.bio: Clearchus of Soli was a Greek philosopher of the 4th-3rd century BCE, belonging to Aristotle's Peripatetic school. He was born in Soli in Cyprus.

Q738027.bio: Hermogenes of Tarsus was a Greek rhetorician, surnamed The Polisher.

Q738057.bio: Theodore Prodromos or Prodromus, probably also the same person as the so-called Ptochoprodromos, was a Byzantine writer, well known for his prose and poetry.

Q738605.bio: Boethus was a Stoic philosopher from Sidon, and a pupil of Diogenes of Babylon.

Q738727.bio: Mark of Ephesus was a hesychast theologian of the late Palaiologan period of the Byzantine Empire who became famous for his rejection of the Council of Ferrara-Florence (1438-1439).

Q739812.bio: Philitas of Cos, sometimes spelled Philetas, was a Greek scholar, poet and grammarian during the early Hellenistic period of ancient Greece. He is regarded as the founder of the Hellenistic school of poetry, which flourished in Alexandria after about 323 BCE.

Q739920.bio: John Moschus, surnamed Eucrates, was a Byzantine monk and ascetical writer of Georgian origin. He is primarily known for his writing of the Spiritual Meadow.

Q7413126.bio: Samus or Samius or Simmias, son of Chrysogonus was a Macedonian lyric and epigrammatic poet. He was brought up with Philip V, the son of Demetrius, by whom also he was put to death, but for what reason we are not informed.

Q743993.bio: Crateuas (111-64 BCE), also known as Cratevas, Krateuas, or Kratevas, was a Greek doctor, pharmacologist, and friend of Mithradates VI Eupator.

Q7447948.bio: Seleucus of Alexandria was a Roman-era grammarian. He was nicknamed 'Homeric'.

Q749452.bio: Clinomachus, was a Megarian philosopher from Thurii, Magna Graecia. He is said by Diogenes Laërtius to have been the first who composed treatises on the fundamental principles of dialectics, and is described as the founder of the Dialectical school.

Q7499.bio: Mary or Maria the Jewess, also known as Mary the Prophetess or Maria the Copt (Arabic: مارية القبطية, romanized: Māriyya al-Qibṭiyya), was an early alchemist known from the works of Zosimos of Panopolis (fl. c. 300 CE) and other authors in the Greek alchemical tradition.

Q754890.bio: Athanas of Syracuse was a historical writer who wrote a work on Sicily and Dion of Syracuse that continued the history of Philistus, and was quoted respectfully by the historians Plutarch and Diodorus Siculus.

Q755297.bio: Athenaeus Mechanicus is the author of a book on siegecraft, On Machines. He is identified by modern scholars with Athenaeus of Seleucia, a member of the Peripatetic school active in the mid-to-late 1st century BCE, at Rome and elsewhere.

Q7563126.bio: Sophonias was a Byzantine monk who wrote commentaries or paraphrases of the works of Aristotle including De Anima, Sophistici Elenchi, Prior Analytics, and the Parva Naturalia, which are still extant.

Q757894.bio: Attalus of Rhodes was an ancient Greek grammarian, astronomer, and mathematician, who lived in Rhodes in the 2nd century BCE, and was a contemporary of Hipparchus. He wrote a commentary on the Phaenomena of Aratus.

Q7707029.bio: Teucer of Babylon (also spelled Teukros and Tinkalūŝā) was an ancient Egyptian astrologer of uncertain date, though likely in or before the first century CE. He was most likely of Greek descent.
